figures.caption: Figure 1. UML notation (see ISO TS 19103, Geographic information - Conceptual schema language)
figures.shows: Legend of the UML diagram notation (draw.io SVG, text inside foreignObject). Left column: a role label on an association line from Class #1 to Class #2 (filled arrowhead = navigable association). Multiplicity examples next to 'Class' boxes: no label = 'Only one', '0...*' = 'Zero or more', '0...1' = 'Optional (zero or one)', '1.. *' = 'One or more', 'n' = 'Specific number'. Right column: 'Aggregate class' joined to Class #1..#n ('Aggregation between classes', hollow diamond at the aggregate end) and 'Superclass' with Subclass #1..#n ('Class inheritance (subtyping of classes)'). Labels contain typos ('0...*', 'Associtation').
figures.lesson: Every association end in the later UML diagrams carries a multiplicity; an unlabelled end means exactly one. The role name sits at the target end and equals the XML child element name. Inheritance means the subclass carries everything of the superclass (e.g. everything derived from _OpenDriveElement may carry g_additionalData).
right: Treat an unlabelled association end as exactly 1 (mandatory, single)
Map role names (e.g. +geometry, +lane) directly to XML child element names
Treat '1..*' as 'at least one must be written'
wrong: Reading '0...*' (three dots, a drawing typo) as something other than '0..*'
Assuming an unlabelled end means optional - it means exactly one, so omitting that child produces invalid output
Treating aggregation as reference-by-ID - in OpenDRIVE XML aggregation becomes nested child elements

figures.caption: Figure 2. UML attribute notation
figures.shows: UML class t_header (abstract parent _OpenDriveElement in italics). All attributes public '+': revMajor: integer and revMinor: integer with no multiplicity; name: string [0..1], version: t_header_Version [0..1], date: string [0..1], north/south/east/west: double [0..1], vendor: string [0..1]. revMinor is boxed red 'mandatory attribute'; name boxed cyan 'optional attribute'.
figures.lesson: An attribute without a [0..1] suffix is mandatory and must always be emitted; [0..1] attributes may be omitted entirely. For the header only revMajor and revMinor are required; the bounding box north/south/east/west is optional.
right: Always write <header revMajor="1" revMinor="7">
Omit optional attributes when no value is known instead of writing empty or zero placeholders
Write north/south/east/west only when computed from the real geometry bounds
wrong: Writing name="" or date="" as fillers (an empty string is a value, not absence)
Writing north=0 south=0 east=0 west=0 as defaults - asserts a wrong bounding box
Omitting revMinor because 'version' was written - version is a separate optional attribute

figures.section: 3.1 Positioning of ASAM OpenDRIVE within ASAM activities
figures.caption: Figure 3. Relation between ASAM OpenDRIVE, ASAM OpenCRG, and ASAM OpenSCENARIO
figures.shows: Three product tiles: OpenDRIVE = 'Static Road Network Description' (intersection with lane arrows and traffic lights, no vehicles); plus OpenSCENARIO = 'Dynamic Scenario Description' (same intersection with vehicles and coloured trajectories) equals 'Scenario description, with dynamic and static content'. A curved arrow leads from the OpenDRIVE tile down to OpenCRG = 'Static Road Surface Description' (cobblestones, pothole, lane-marking close-up).
figures.lesson: OpenDRIVE carries only static road-network content (geometry, lanes, signals, objects). Vehicles, routes and trajectories belong to OpenSCENARIO; fine surface texture/roughness (potholes, cobbles) belongs to OpenCRG and is only referenced from OpenDRIVE.
right: Emit static network only: roads, lanes, junctions, signals, static objects
Represent detailed surface roughness only via <surface><CRG> references, if at all
wrong: Encoding traffic flow, routes or vehicles in OpenDRIVE - that is OpenSCENARIO content
Modelling potholes or paving texture with elevation/shape polynomials - surface detail is OpenCRG's job

figures.section: 5.1 User Data / 5.2 Including Data / 5.4 Description of the data quality (Core UML)
figures.caption: Figure 4. UML model ASAM OpenDRIVE Core
figures.shows: UML 'class Core'. t_OpenDRIVE (orange) has: +header (no multiplicity = exactly 1) t_header, +road 1..* Road::t_road, +controller 0..* Signal::t_controller, +junction 0..* Junction::t_junction, +junctionGroup 0..* Junction::t_junctionGroup, +station 0..* Railroad::t_station (blue = other packages). All generalise (hollow triangle) to abstract _OpenDriveElement, which has g_additionalData 0..* (t_OpenDRIVE also links to it 0..*). g_additionalData groups +userData 0..* t_userData (code: string mandatory, value: string [0..1], 0..* userDataContent), +include 0..* t_include (file: string), +dataQuality 0..1 t_dataQuality. t_dataQuality has +error 0..1 t_dataQuality_Error (xyAbsolute, xyRelative, zAbsolute, zRelative: double, all mandatory) and +rawData 0..1 t_dataQuality_RawData (date: string, postProcessing: enum, source: enum mandatory; postProcessingComment, sourceComment [0..1]). Separate primitive types t_zeroOne, t_grEqZero, t_grZero, all specialisations of double.
figures.lesson: A valid file needs exactly one header and at least one road; junctions/controllers are optional. Any element (not only the root) may carry userData/include/dataQuality, so provenance (e.g. the OSM way id) can be attached per road/lane/object. If <error> is written, all four error values are mandatory. t_grZero = strictly > 0, t_grEqZero = >= 0, t_zeroOne = [0,1].
right: Always emit one <header> and at least one <road>
Attach OSM provenance as <userData code="osm_way_id" value="..."/> on the element it describes
If writing <dataQuality><error>, provide xyAbsolute, xyRelative, zAbsolute and zRelative together
In <rawData> always give date, source and postProcessing; name OpenStreetMap in sourceComment
wrong: Producing a file with zero roads (violates road 1..*)
Writing only xyAbsolute in <error> - the other three are mandatory
Assuming userData is only allowed at file level
Treating t_grZero fields (e.g. geometry length) as allowing 0

figures.caption: Figure 5. Available coordinate systems in ASAM OpenDRIVE
figures.shows: Three identical right-handed axis triads side by side: Inertial System (x blue forward-right, y green to the left, z red up), Reference Line System (s forward, t left, h up), Local System (u forward, v left, z up).
figures.lesson: All three systems share the same handedness and layout: the second axis (y, t, v) points LEFT of the first, the third points up. +t / +v is left of the direction of s / u, and positive rotations are counter-clockwise seen from above.
right: Left normal for +t: n = (-sin hdg, cos hdg)
Treat s->t->h exactly like x->y->z (right-handed)
wrong: Using a screen convention with y down, or t pointing right - mirrors every lane
Feeding a left-handed engine convention (e.g. Unreal/CARLA with y to the right) without converting - flips t, headings and curvature signs
figures.formula: t-unit = (-sin(hdg), cos(hdg)); h = s x t

figures.caption: Figure 6. Coordinate systems in ASAM OpenDRIVE interacting with another
figures.shows: Inertial X/Y grid with a blue reference line curving to the upper right. At a point labelled 'reference line system' s is tangent to the line and t perpendicular pointing up-left. A grey segment leads down-right to a 'local system' point, with a right-angle mark between this segment and the tangent; at the local origin u points down-right and v up-right, i.e. the local frame is rotated relative to s/t.
figures.lesson: A local origin is found by going to s on the reference line and then moving perpendicular to the tangent by t (here t < 0, i.e. to the right). The local axes may additionally carry their own heading relative to s/t.
right: Place objects/signals at P = refline(s) + t * leftNormal(s)
Apply an object's heading on top of the reference-line heading at s
wrong: Offsetting t along the inertial y-axis instead of perpendicular to the tangent
Assuming the local u axis is aligned with s - only true when the local heading is 0
figures.formula: P(s,t) = (x(s) - t*sin(hdg(s)), y(s) + t*cos(hdg(s)))

figures.caption: Figure 7. Inertial coordinate system with defined rotations
figures.shows: Three-step rotation sequence. Panel 1 'heading > 0': rotation about z (z = z'), x turns counter-clockwise to x', y to y'. Panel 2 'heading = 0, pitch > 0': rotation about y' (y' = y''); x'' is drawn BELOW x' (tips down) and z'' leans toward the former x direction. Panel 3 'heading = 0, pitch = 0, roll > 0': rotation about x'' (x'' = x'''); y''' is lifted ABOVE y'' and z''' leans away from y (toward the right).
figures.lesson: Rotation order is heading (about z), then pitch (about the new y'), then roll (about the new x''). All angles follow the right-hand rule: positive heading = counter-clockwise from above; positive pitch = nose DOWN (x tips toward -z); positive roll = left side (+y) UP, right side down.
right: Build R = Rz(heading) * Ry(pitch) * Rx(roll) (intrinsic z, y', x'')
An object whose front points uphill has NEGATIVE pitch
An object banked with its left side higher has positive roll
wrong: Using the aviation/graphics habit 'positive pitch = nose up' - inverts every slope
Applying roll before pitch/heading, or using extrinsic rotations
Treating heading as a compass bearing (north = 0, clockwise) instead of a CCW angle from +x (east)
figures.formula: R = Rz(h)*Ry(p)*Rx(r); pitch=+pi/2 -> x'' = -z; roll=+pi/2 -> z''' = -y''

figures.caption: Figure 8. Inertial coordinate system with defined rotations
figures.shows: Four box sketches seen from the front (x toward the viewer, y left, z up). (a) all angles 0: only y and z visible. (b) heading < 0: x' appears pointing to the viewer's right and a side face becomes visible, z' = z. (c) heading < 0, pitch < 0: the box tilts so its top face is visible; x'' points right and upward, y'' = y'. (d) heading < 0, pitch < 0, roll > 0: additionally rolled - z''' leans right and the left (y''') edge is raised, x''' = x''.
figures.lesson: Same convention as Figure 7, demonstrated with negative angles: negative heading = clockwise from above (x turns toward -y); negative pitch = front lifts up; positive roll = +y side up.
right: Use negative heading for a clockwise yaw from +x
Use negative pitch for an object whose front points upward
wrong: Reading pitch < 0 as nose down - it is nose up
Interpreting heading < 0 as turning left

figures.caption: Figure 9. Reference line coordinate system
figures.shows: Inertial X/Y grid (x = 1..7, y = 1..6) with an S-shaped grey road. A dashed reference line runs down its middle with labels s = 0 .. s = 8 at equal spacing along the line; dashed cross-lines at each tick run perpendicular to the line across the road. At s = 0 (about x = 2.2, y = 1.2) a blue s arrow points along the line and a green t arrow perpendicular to its left. Between neighbouring ticks the outer edge of each bend is visibly longer than the inner edge.
figures.lesson: s is arc length ALONG the reference line (in the xy-plane), starting at 0 at the road start; t is measured perpendicular to the local tangent, positive left. Because cross-sections are perpendicular to the reference line, equal ds maps to unequal lengths on lane borders (longer outside a bend, shorter inside).
right: Parameterise lanes, objects and signals by reference-line arc length s starting at 0 for each road
Compute lane-border lengths separately when needed (e.g. marking dash spacing) - they differ from ds
Keep |t * curvature| < 1 so cross-sections do not cross on the inside of bends
wrong: Using chord length or straight OSM node-to-node distances as s on curved geometry
Continuing s from the previous road (s restarts at 0 for every road)
Applying lane widths along x or y instead of along the normal
figures.formula: offset-curve length element: dl = (1 - t*kappa(s)) ds

figures.caption: Figure 10. Reference line system with defined rotations
figures.shows: Two panels. Left: heading rotation about h (h = h'); s turns counter-clockwise to s', t to t'. Right: roll about s (s = s'''); t''' lifted above t, h''' leans away from t (to the right). No pitch panel exists.
figures.lesson: The reference-line frame has only two rotational degrees of freedom: heading (from planView geometry) and roll (from superelevation). There is no pitch - elevation lifts the frame vertically without tilting s.
right: Derive the s/t/h frame from planView heading and superelevation roll only
Positive superelevation = left (+t) side up
wrong: Pitching the s-axis with the elevation gradient when computing t-offsets or lane widths
Treating superelevation as positive when the right side is raised

figures.caption: Figure 11. Heading in reference line
figures.shows: Inertial X/Y grid with a grey reference line rising to the right. At its start s points slightly up-right and t up-left; at a later point s' and t' are rotated more steeply, following the tangent. Text in the frame: 'Heading caused by <geometry>'.
figures.lesson: The reference-line heading at any s comes solely from planView geometry (start hdg of the containing geometry plus accumulated curvature) and varies continuously along curved geometry.
right: Evaluate heading at s from the containing <geometry> (hdg + integral of curvature)
Ensure heading continuity at geometry boundaries
wrong: Using a single heading per road
Taking heading from raw OSM segment directions without smoothing (kinks)
figures.formula: hdg(s) = hdg0 + integral from s0 to s of kappa(u) du

figures.caption: Figure 12. Roll in reference line
figures.shows: Cross-section of the road seen looking along +s (s is the blue dot at height 0 on an axis labelled 'Z'; the horizontal axis is labelled 'X'). A thick road line passes through s, higher on the LEFT where the green t arrow points and lower on the right. An arc marks the roll angle between the horizontal and the road line; the dashed vertical h is rotated to h', which leans right. Text: 'Roll caused by <superelevation>'.
figures.lesson: Superelevation is a roll of the s/t/h frame about s; positive roll raises the left (+t) side and tilts h toward -t. The pivot is the reference line (t = 0): points with t > 0 rise and t < 0 drop by t*tan(roll).
right: Lateral height: z = z_ref(s) + t*tan(superelevation(s)) (plus lateral shape)
A right-hand curve (negative curvature) is banked left-side-high, i.e. positive superelevation
wrong: Pivoting the bank around the road edge instead of the reference line
Sign error: raising the right side for positive superelevation
Reading the horizontal 'X' label literally - the section lies in the t-h plane, with t to the left
figures.formula: dz(t) = t * tan(roll(s))

figures.caption: Figure 13. Elevation in reference line
figures.shows: Side view: vertical z axis with 0 marked; a grey elevation curve is flat at z = 0, rises smoothly, then levels off. Two s/t/h frames are drawn, one at z = 0 and one on the rising part; in BOTH s is horizontal and h vertical - the frame is translated up, not tilted. Text: '<elevation> projected on reference line'.
figures.lesson: Elevation only shifts the reference-line frame vertically; the frame is never pitched, and s remains the horizontal (xy-projected) arc length. A 10 % grade over 100 m of s still has s-length 100 m, not 100.5 m.
right: Compute s and geometry @length purely in 2D
Evaluate z(s) from the elevation polynomial and translate (never rotate) the s/t frame
wrong: Using 3D arc length (including climb) as s or as geometry length
Pitching lanes/objects with the slope when computing lateral positions
Fitting elevation polynomials against 3D distance instead of planar s
figures.formula: z(s) = a + b*ds + c*ds^2 + d*ds^3 with ds = s - s_start; s measured in the xy-plane

figures.caption: Figure 14. Local system with defined rotations
figures.shows: Same three-panel rotation drawing as Figure 7 with u/v/z: heading about z (u -> u' counter-clockwise), pitch about v (v = v''; u'' tips down, z'' leans forward), roll about u (u = u'''; v''' lifted, z''' leans right).
figures.lesson: The local (object) frame uses the identical heading-pitch-roll convention as the inertial frame: heading CCW positive about z, positive pitch = front (u) down, positive roll = left (v) side up, applied in the order heading, pitch, roll.
right: Reuse the same rotation code for local and inertial frames
wrong: Using different sign conventions for object orientation than for the inertial system
figures.formula: R_local = Rz(heading)*Ry(pitch)*Rx(roll)

figures.caption: Figure 15. Local coordinate systems with heading, pitch, roll
figures.shows: Four box sketches identical to Figure 8 but labelled u/v/z: all zero; heading < 0 (u' to the viewer's right); heading < 0 and pitch < 0 (top face visible, u'' pointing right and up, v'' = v'); plus roll > 0 (left edge raised, u''' = u'').
figures.lesson: Confirms local angle signs match the inertial convention: negative heading = clockwise, negative pitch lifts the front, positive roll lifts the left side.
right: Same sign handling as Figure 8 for objects placed in local coordinates
wrong: Interpreting a local heading as a compass bearing

figures.caption: Figure 16. Local coordinate system with respect to reference line system
figures.shows: Inertial grid with blue reference line; reference-line system at a point with s along the tangent and t up-left (right angle marked). A local origin lies below-right of it (t < 0). At the local origin an unrotated pair u (parallel to s) / v (parallel to t, solid green) is drawn plus a rotated pair u'/v' (dashed) turned counter-clockwise, with an arrow marking the angle from u to u'. Text: 'Heading of local coordinate system with respect to reference line coordinate system'.
figures.lesson: An object's local heading is measured relative to the reference-line tangent at its s, not relative to inertial east. Heading 0 means the object faces +s; the unrotated local frame is parallel to s/t at the projected point.
right: Inertial yaw of an object = hdg_refline(s) + object.hdg
Express orientation of OSM point features relative to the road tangent
wrong: Writing an absolute (inertial or compass) yaw into object @hdg - wrong on any road not running due east
Trusting the phrase '0.0 = east' in the 6.4 text - the figure shows the heading is relative to s
figures.formula: yaw_inertial = hdg_ref(s) + hdg_local

figures.section: 6.5 Summary of all available coordinate systems
figures.caption: Figure 17. Summary of coordinate system in ASAM OpenDRIVE
figures.shows: Perspective sketch: inertial system at lower left (x, y, z); a blue reference line with a reference-line system at one point (s tangent, t left, h up); dashed lines project that point onto the inertial x and y directions; a local system (u, v, z) beside the reference line, linked to the reference point by dashed lines and slightly rotated relative to s/t.
figures.lesson: The systems are chained: inertial -> reference line (via geometry x, y, hdg plus elevation/superelevation at s) -> local (via s, t, zOffset and local heading/pitch/roll). Local placements are never given directly in inertial coordinates.
right: Implement local->s/t/h->x/y/z as a composition of two transforms
Convert OSM point features to (s, t) by projecting onto the nearest road reference line
wrong: Writing inertial x/y directly into s/t attributes
Ignoring reference-line elevation/roll when converting local z to inertial z
figures.formula: X_obj = X_ref(s) + R_ref(s)*([0, t, 0] + R_local*p_local)

figures.caption: Figure 18. geoReference and offset
figures.shows: Inertial X/Y plot with broken axes. Lower left: an S-shaped road in 'OpenDRIVE x/y coordinates' (x about 10-45, y about 10-35), its start marked with a red circle near (15, 10) and small s/t arrows. Upper right: the identical, unrotated road in 'Geo referenced x/y coordinates' (x about 500000-500030, y about 40005-40030), start also circled. Brackets 'x offset' and 'y offset' span the distance between the two start points.
figures.lesson: The header <offset> is a translation from small, numerically safe OpenDRIVE coordinates to projected map coordinates (e.g. UTM easting incl. its 500000 m false easting): projected = OpenDRIVE + offset. The figure shows no rotation, consistent with the rule that @hdg should be avoided.
right: Store geometry near (0,0) and write <offset x=E0 y=N0 z=Z0 hdg="0"/> in the header
Keep <geoReference> as the unmodified EPSG/PROJ string (with its own +x_0/+y_0)
Recover map coordinates as E = x + offset.x, N = y + offset.y
wrong: Writing raw UTM coordinates (~5e5, ~5e6) into geometry @x/@y (precision loss; against the rule)
Folding the offset into the proj string by editing +x_0/+y_0
Subtracting the offset when converting to map coordinates (sign inversion)
Using a non-zero offset @hdg
figures.formula: x_geo = x_odr + offset.x; y_geo = y_odr + offset.y (with hdg = 0)

figures.caption: Figure 19. Geometry elements in ASAM OpenDRIVE
figures.shows: Five matplotlib thumbnails: 'straight lines' (line from (0,0) to (5,1.25)), 'spirals' (clothoid curling inward), 'arcs' (arc rising and flattening), 'cubic polynomials' (y(x) cubic with a local wiggle on x in [-4,4]), 'Parametric cubic polynomials' (curve bending gently down from 0 to about -0.6 over about 60 m).
figures.lesson: Exactly five planView primitives exist: line, spiral, arc, poly3 (deprecated) and paramPoly3. Prefer line/arc/spiral (exact, curvature-continuous) or paramPoly3 for free-form fits.
right: Emit line/spiral/arc for designed shapes and paramPoly3 for smoothed measured polylines
wrong: Emitting new poly3 geometry (deprecated in 1.7)
Approximating curves with many tiny lines (curvature jumps and heading kinks)

figures.caption: Figure 20. The individual parts of a road
figures.shows: Top row: 'reference line' + 'lanes' + 'features' = composite road. Bottom: perspective view of a two-lane road; the blue reference line runs between a yellow lane labelled '1' (left) and a blue lane labelled '-1' (right). Arrows at the bottom: s along the reference line away from the viewer, t pointing left. Speed-limit signs '60' (far) and '80' (near) stand on the right roadside.
figures.lesson: A road is three layers: reference line (geometry), lanes defined relative to it, and features (signals/objects) placed in s/t. Lanes left of the reference line (+t) have positive IDs, right lanes negative IDs; the reference line is the zero-width centre lane 0 between them.
right: Put the reference line on the boundary between left and right lanes for two-way roads
Number lanes 1, 2, ... outward on the left and -1, -2, ... outward on the right
Place right-roadside signals with t < 0
wrong: Giving right-side lanes positive IDs
Assuming the reference-line direction implies driving direction (the text says it does not)

figures.caption: Figure 21. UML model Road Geometry including the Reference Line elements
figures.shows: UML 'class RoadGeometry'. t_road_planView has +geometry 1..* t_road_planView_geometry (hdg: double, length: t_grZero, s: t_grEqZero, x: double, y: double) with children +line (no attributes), +spiral (curvEnd, curvStart: double), +arc (curvature: double), +poly3 (a, b, c, d), +paramPoly3 (aU, aV, bU, bV, cU, cV, dU, dV: double, pRange: e_paramPoly3_pRange - no [0..1], i.e. mandatory). t_road_lateralProfile has +superelevation 0..* (a, b, c, d, s: t_grEqZero) and +shape 0..* (a, b, c, d, s, t). t_road_elevationProfile has +elevation 0..* (a, b, c, d, s). t_road_surface has +CRG 0..* (file, mode, orientation, sStart, sEnd mandatory; hOffset, purpose, sOffset, tOffset, zOffset, zScale optional).
figures.lesson: Every planView needs at least one geometry; geometry length must be strictly > 0 (t_grZero), s >= 0. paramPoly3 must always carry pRange. Elevation, superelevation and shape records are optional.
right: Drop or merge zero-length segments before writing geometry
Always write pRange="arcLength" or "normalized" on paramPoly3
Write geometry records in ascending s, starting at 0
wrong: Emitting <geometry length="0"> for degenerate OSM segments
Omitting pRange and relying on a reader default
Writing two primitives inside one <geometry>

figures.caption: Figure 22. A straight line
figures.shows: matplotlib plot of one straight segment from about (-47, 1) to about (-1.7, 35.7) m; axes 'x-axis [m]', 'y-axis [m]'. It matches the XML example: x = -47.17, y = 0.728, hdg = 0.6548 rad, length = 57.28 (end = (-1.6, 35.4)).
figures.lesson: A line is fully defined by start (x, y), hdg and length; the end point follows. hdg is the mathematical angle from +x (0.655 rad ~ 37.5 deg, north-east).
right: End = start + length*(cos hdg, sin hdg)
Use that end as the next geometry's start (no leaps)
wrong: Storing end coordinates instead of length
Writing hdg in degrees
figures.formula: x(ds) = x0 + ds*cos(hdg); y(ds) = y0 + ds*sin(hdg)

figures.caption: Figure 23. Road geometry described by a spiral
figures.shows: matplotlib plot (sub-metre scale) of a clothoid starting at (0, 0) heading straight up (+y) with zero curvature, bending right (clockwise) with ever-increasing curvature over the top near (0.43, 0.78), down past (0.72, 0.5) and curling inward to end near (0.34, 0.49) - more than a full turn. Not drawn from the XML example values.
figures.lesson: A spiral's curvature changes linearly with arc length; as |curvature| grows it winds into an ever-tighter curl. Clockwise winding = negative curvature (right curve). Position requires Fresnel-type integration; an arc approximation is wrong.
right: kappa(ds) = curvStart + (curvEnd - curvStart)*ds/length
Evaluate via Fresnel integrals or accurate numeric integration
Use negative curvature values for right-hand transitions
wrong: Approximating a spiral by an arc with average curvature
Assuming spirals must start or end at curvature 0
Writing curvStart = curvEnd (rule: should differ - use an arc)
figures.formula: kappa(ds) = cS + (cE - cS)*ds/L; hdg(ds) = hdg0 + cS*ds + (cE - cS)*ds^2/(2L); x = x0 + int cos(hdg) ds; y = y0 + int sin(hdg) ds

figures.caption: Figure 24. Road geometry described by an arc
figures.shows: matplotlib plot of an arc starting near (0, 72) heading east (+x) and bending clockwise down to about (70.5, 12.5); radius about 71-72 m with the centre near the origin (a single dot is plotted at (0, 0)); sweep about 80 deg. Not drawn from the XML example (example curvature -0.127 1/m).
figures.lesson: An arc has constant curvature = 1/R; a clockwise (right-turning) arc has negative curvature and its centre lies on the -t (right) side at distance R from the start.
right: curvature = -1/R for right curves, +1/R for left curves
Centre = start + (1/kappa)*(-sin hdg, cos hdg)
wrong: Writing positive curvature for a clockwise arc
Writing curvature 0 (use <line>)
Writing radius instead of curvature
figures.formula: x = x0 + (sin(hdg0 + k*ds) - sin(hdg0))/k; y = y0 - (cos(hdg0 + k*ds) - cos(hdg0))/k

figures.section: 7.5 Generating arbitrary road courses from geometry elements
figures.caption: Figure 25. Creating a reference line from geometry elements
figures.shows: Left: five colour-coded pieces in order - line (orange), spiral (blue), arc (green), spiral (blue), arc (green). Right: they are chained into one smooth reference line bending left toward the upper right, with s/t frames at start (t up-left) and end (s pointing up, t pointing left). Bottom: curvature-vs-s plot - 0 along the line, linear ramp up (spiral), constant (arc), linear ramp DOWN to a smaller but still positive value (spiral), constant (arc); steering-wheel icons show straight, turning left, held, partly unwound, held.
figures.lesson: Geometry elements are concatenated so that position, heading AND curvature are continuous; spirals play the role of turning the steering wheel between different curvatures, including arc-to-arc transitions between two non-zero curvatures. Positive curvature = left turn.
right: Insert spirals between line and arc and between arcs of different radius
Check position, heading and curvature continuity at every geometry join
Use spirals with non-zero curvStart and curvEnd for compound curves
wrong: Line directly followed by arc (curvature jump - allowed but not recommended)
Assuming spiral curvature always returns to zero
Heading mismatch at joins producing kinks
figures.formula: kappa(s) piecewise linear and continuous

figures.caption: Figure 26. A cubic polynom
figures.shows: matplotlib plot of y(x) for x in [-100, 100] m: starts at y = -75, flattens to a plateau near y = 20 around x = 0, climbs to y = 125 at x = 100. Coefficients a = 20, b = 0, c = 0.0005, d = 0.0001.
figures.lesson: A plain cubic in inertial x/y is a function y(x): one y per x. This is only background; <poly3> is evaluated in a local u/v frame.
wrong: Evaluating <poly3> coefficients against inertial x instead of local u
figures.formula: y(x) = a + b*x + c*x^2 + d*x^3

figures.caption: Figure 27. A curve which cannot be represented by a cubic polynom w.r.t x parameter
figures.shows: Inertial X/Y grid with a curve from (3, 1.5) rising and bending back over itself near x = 5; a vertical red line at x ~ 4.85 hits the curve twice (y ~ 3.3 and y ~ 4.3). Warning icon and text 'two Y-values for one X-value'.
figures.lesson: A curve that turns back in x cannot be written as y(x); poly3 must be expressed in a rotated local frame where it is a single-valued function of u, so u must increase monotonically along the curve.
right: Choose the local u axis along the start heading so v(u) is single-valued
Use paramPoly3 when the heading changes by ~90 deg or more relative to the start
wrong: Fitting poly3 in global x
Using poly3 where u would not be monotonic

figures.caption: Figure 28. Transformation from a u/v- to a x/y coordinate system with a=b=0
figures.shows: Inertial grid; poly3 starts at (3, 1.45) with s/t arrows; orange u axis along the start heading (angle 'hdg' from horizontal) and v axis perpendicular to the left. A curve point near (5, 4.5) is decomposed into u (along u) and v(u) (perpendicular) and into inertial x(u), y(u). Text: 'Cubic polynom with a = b = 0', 'For every u-value only one v-value is possible', and formulas beta = hdg + arctan(v(u)/u), x(u) = x(u=0) + sqrt(u^2 + v(u)^2)*cos(beta), y(u) = y(u=0) + sqrt(u^2 + v(u)^2)*sin(beta).
figures.lesson: With a = b = 0 the u/v frame coincides with s/t at the start: origin = (x, y), u along hdg, v to the left. A curve point is the start plus the local (u, v) vector rotated by hdg; the polar form shown is just a rotation.
right: x = x0 + u*cos(hdg) - v*sin(hdg); y = y0 + u*sin(hdg) + v*cos(hdg)
Use a rotation matrix or atan2, not arctan(v/u)
Write a = b = 0 for smooth reference lines
wrong: Implementing beta = hdg + arctan(v/u) literally - divides by zero at u = 0 and loses the quadrant if u < 0
Treating u as arc length (u is a projection; @length is the curve length)
figures.formula: beta = hdg + atan2(v,u); x = x0 + sqrt(u^2+v^2)cos(beta); y = y0 + sqrt(u^2+v^2)sin(beta); v(u) = a + b*u + c*u^2 + d*u^3

figures.caption: Figure 29. Transformation from a u/v- to a x/y coordinate system with a!=0 and b!=0
figures.shows: Despite the poly3 caption it is drawn with paramPoly3 labels (practically identical to Figure 32): a u/v frame whose origin (orange dot near (2.6, 0.45)) is offset from the geometry start (x(p=0), y(p=0)) ~ (3.05, 1.45); the start lies at u = aU, v = aV in that frame (segments labelled 'aU', 'aV'). The u axis is inclined by 'hdg' to the horizontal; the curve's initial tangent (s arrow) is inclined a further 'arctan(bV/bU)' relative to u. A curve point near (4.8, 4.8) is decomposed into u(p), v(p) and x(u), y(u).
figures.lesson: Non-zero a terms (aU/aV) shift the curve start away from the u/v origin and a non-zero bV rotates the start tangent away from hdg; hdg is then the orientation of the u axis, not of the curve. Start point, hdg and true tangent stop agreeing - avoid this.
right: Write aU = aV = bV = 0, bU > 0 (and poly3 a = b = 0) so (x, y, hdg) are the true start point and tangent
Initial tangent angle = hdg + atan2(bV, bU)
wrong: Emitting non-zero aU/aV/bV - readers disagree on whether (x, y) is the u/v origin or the curve start, giving shifted roads
Assuming hdg is the curve's start tangent when bV != 0
Taking this poly3-captioned figure as poly3 semantics (it shows paramPoly3 parameters; the poly3 text puts (x, y) at u = 0 on the v axis)
figures.formula: tangent0 = hdg + atan2(bV, bU); point = origin_uv + R(hdg)*(u(p), v(p))

figures.section: 7.7.1 Generating roads using parametric cubic curves
figures.caption: Figure 30. A parametric cubic polynom for interpolation of u coordinate
figures.shows: Plot of u versus parameter p (p = 1..7): cubic starting at u = aU ~ 1.4 with initial slope angle 'arctan(bU)', rising to a maximum ~3.4 near p ~ 3.3 and then falling to ~2.85 at p ~ 4.85. A red marker at (p ~ 4.85, u ~ 4.3) with lines labelled 'p' and 'u(p)' is NOT on the drawn curve (schematic inconsistency).
figures.lesson: u is an independent cubic in p: u(0) = aU, du/dp(0) = bU. u need not be monotonic in p, so the curve may move backwards in u (which poly3 cannot).
right: u(p) = aU + bU p + cU p^2 + dU p^3, evaluated independently of v
For smooth reference lines use aU = 0, bU = 1 with pRange = arcLength
wrong: Reading values off this schematic (the marked point is inconsistent with the curve)
Assuming u(p) is monotonic
figures.formula: u(p) = aU + bU*p + cU*p^2 + dU*p^3

figures.section: 7.7.1 Generating roads using parametric cubic curves
figures.caption: Figure 31. A parametric cubic polynom for interpolation of v coordinate
figures.shows: Plot of v versus p: cubic starting at v = aV ~ 2.6 with small initial slope angle 'arctan(bV)', rising monotonically to ~4.3 at p ~ 4.85, marked by a red point with lines labelled 'p' and 'v(p)'.
figures.lesson: v is an independent cubic in p: v(0) = aV, dv/dp(0) = bV. It is the lateral deviation from the start tangent; with bV = 0 the curve leaves exactly along hdg.
right: v(p) = aV + bV p + cV p^2 + dV p^3
Use bV = 0 for tangent-continuous joins
wrong: Non-zero bV producing a heading kink against the previous geometry
figures.formula: v(p) = aV + bV*p + cV*p^2 + dV*p^3

figures.section: 7.7.1 Generating roads using parametric cubic curves
figures.caption: Figure 32. A parametric cubic polynom
figures.shows: Same drawing as Figure 29: u/v frame origin (orange dot) offset from the start point by aU (along u) and aV (along v); u axis rotated by hdg; initial curve tangent rotated a further arctan(bV/bU); a curve point decomposed into u(p), v(p) and inertial x(u), y(u).
figures.lesson: paramPoly3 evaluates u(p), v(p), rotates by hdg and translates into the inertial frame. p is NOT arc length except at the endpoints for pRange = arcLength; the true curve length (numerical integral) must match @length. Aligned form: aU = aV = bV = 0, bU > 0.
right: x = x0 + u cos hdg - v sin hdg; y = y0 + u sin hdg + v cos hdg (with aU = aV = 0)
Compute @length by numerically integrating |(u'(p), v'(p))| over the p range
Invert p(s) numerically for s lookups instead of assuming p = s
wrong: Assuming p equals arc length in the interior
Setting @length to the chord length, or to 1 when pRange = normalized
Non-zero aU/aV (ambiguous start point)
figures.formula: x(p) = x0 + u(p)cos(hdg) - v(p)sin(hdg); y(p) = y0 + u(p)sin(hdg) + v(p)cos(hdg); length = integral sqrt(u'(p)^2 + v'(p)^2) dp

figures.section: 8. Roads (road element UML, after the t_road attribute table)
figures.caption: Figure 33. UML Model for Roads
figures.shows: UML class diagram of t_road: attributes name[0..1], length (t_grZero, >0), id (string), junction (string), rule (e_trafficRule [0..1]). Children with multiplicities: link 0..1, lanes exactly 1, objects 0..1, signals 0..1, railroad 0..1, type 0..* (t_road_type: s, type, country[0..1]; with speed 0..1 -> max, unit), surface 0..1, lateralProfile 0..1, elevationProfile 0..1, planView exactly 1. Also lists e_countryCode variants (alpha2 current; alpha3 and old codes deprecated) and t_maxSpeed = t_grEqZero or e_maxSpeedString.
figures.lesson: Every road needs exactly one planView and exactly one lanes element; everything else is optional. junction is mandatory as an attribute (use "-1" when not a connecting road). length must be strictly positive. Road type entries are a sequence keyed by s, each may carry one speed child.
right: Always emit <planView> and <lanes> per road
Always write junction="-1" for normal roads
Use ISO 3166 alpha-2 country codes on <type>
Write <type s=..> entries in ascending s, speed as child of type
wrong: Omitting <lanes> or <planView> - multiplicity 1 means schema-invalid
Writing length=0 for degenerate OSM ways - t_grZero forbids it; drop or merge zero-length segments
Using alpha-3 country codes - deprecated in 1.7

figures.section: 8. Roads / 8.3 Road reference line geometry (UML for planView, lateralProfile, elevationProfile, surface)
figures.caption: Figure 34. UML model for Road Geometry
figures.shows: UML: planView has 1..* geometry (s, x, y, hdg, length>0) each holding exactly one of line / spiral(curvStart, curvEnd) / arc(curvature) / poly3(a..d, deprecated) / paramPoly3(aU..dU, aV..dV, pRange). lateralProfile has 0..* superelevation(s,a,b,c,d) and 0..* shape(s,t,a,b,c,d). elevationProfile has 0..* elevation(s,a,b,c,d). surface has 0..* CRG(file, sStart, sEnd, orientation, mode, purpose, sOffset, tOffset, zOffset, zScale, hOffset).
figures.lesson: Geometry, elevation, superelevation and shape are all piecewise cubic records keyed by s (shape additionally by t). A geometry record carries its own start pose (x,y,hdg) and length; there is no implicit chaining - the writer must make poses consistent.
right: Emit at least one <geometry>; each with exactly one primitive child
Shape records need both s and t
paramPoly3 needs pRange (arcLength or normalized)
wrong: Emitting poly3 for new data - deprecated; prefer paramPoly3
Computing geometry s values that do not equal the accumulated sum of previous lengths - consumers rely on contiguous s

figures.caption: Figure 35. Allowed, prohibited, and recommended road linkage
figures.shows: Four panels, each two roads with lanes 1 (yellow, left of reference line) and -1 (blue, right), blue arrow = reference line direction. Top-left: reference lines do not touch (gap) - red X. Top-right: the first reference line runs past the start of the second (overlap) - red X. Bottom-left: reference lines meet exactly at one point but the roads have a heading kink, so the lane areas show a gap on the outer side and an overlap on the inner side - yellow warning triangle (allowed, not recommended). Bottom-right: roads join with a common point and common tangent, lanes flush - green tick (recommended).
figures.lesson: Linked roads must share the endpoint of their reference lines exactly (G0). Tangent continuity (G1) is recommended; a heading kink is tolerated but produces lane gap/overlap wedges.
right: End point of predecessor reference line == start point of successor reference line
Same heading at the joint so lane polygons are flush
wrong: Reference line gap between linked roads - prohibited
Reference line overlap (one road extends past the other's start) - prohibited
Heading kink at the joint - allowed but creates lane gaps/overlaps; avoid by smoothing OSM polylines into G1 geometry

figures.caption: Figure 36. Allowed scenarios of road linkage
figures.shows: Four panels with Road 1 (left) and Road 2 (right), lanes labelled per road. (a) Both reference lines run left-to-right: Road1 successor = 2 contactPoint start; Road2 predecessor = 1 contactPoint end. (b) Road 1 reference line points left (its lane -1 is on top, 1 below), Road 2 points right: both STARTS meet; Road1 predecessor = 2 start, Road2 predecessor = 1 start; successors n.a. (c) Road 1 points right, Road 2 points left (Road2 lane -1 on top, 1 below): both ENDS meet; Road1 successor = 2 end, Road2 successor = 1 end. (d) Red X: Road 1 has lanes 2,1,-1 with its reference line drawn between lanes 2 and 1, Road 2 has lanes 2,1,-1 with reference line between 1 and -1 - the two reference lines are laterally displaced at the joint, so they do not connect.
figures.lesson: Predecessor/successor is about the START/END of the road's own reference line, and contactPoint says which END of the other road touches. Opposite-direction roads can be linked directly (start-start or end-end); lane ids flip sign across such a joint because left/right swap. Reference lines must coincide at the joint; you cannot compensate a lateral jump of the reference line by renumbering lanes.
right: Head-to-tail: succ contactPoint=start / pred contactPoint=end
Start-to-start: both use predecessor, contactPoint=start
End-to-end: both use successor, contactPoint=end
If OSM way directions oppose, keep the roads and link with matching contact points instead of reversing geometry
wrong: Assuming successor always has contactPoint=start
Linking roads whose reference lines are laterally offset at the joint (e.g. reference line on a different lane boundary) - not a valid link; use a laneOffset to move lanes, or a junction
Leaving out the reciprocal link on the other road (the tables always fill both roads)

figures.caption: Figure 37. Allowed scenario of road linkage within a junction
figures.shows: An incoming road with lanes -1 and -2 (one direction, arrows right) enters a dashed junction box. Inside are two connecting roads: one curving up-right carrying a single lane -1 starting from incoming lane -1, and one straight carrying lane -1 starting from incoming lane -2. The straight connecting road continues into an outgoing road with one lane -1. Each connecting road has its own reference line starting exactly at the incoming road's endpoint area.
figures.lesson: When one road splits into several, the split must be modelled as a junction with one connecting road per path; each connecting road has its own reference line, can carry a subset of lanes and renumbers them from its own centre lane (incoming -2 becomes -1 on the straight connector).
right: Use a junction for one-to-many road splits
Connecting roads carry only the lanes needed for that path and number them from their own centre (-1, -2, ...)
Connecting road reference line starts on the incoming road's end cross-section
wrong: Linking one road directly to two successor roads without a junction - road link is 1:1
Copying incoming lane ids into the connector (lane -2 kept as -2 with an empty -1)

figures.caption: Figure 38. UML model for road linkage
figures.shows: UML: t_road_link has predecessor 0..1 and successor 0..1 of type t_road_link_predecessorSuccessor with elementId (required), elementType (road/junction), contactPoint [0..1], elementS [0..1], elementDir [0..1].
figures.lesson: A road has at most one predecessor and one successor. contactPoint is optional in the schema but required in practice when elementType=road (and absent when linking to a junction, which uses no contact point); elementS/elementDir are only for virtual junctions.
right: elementType=road -> give contactPoint
elementType=junction -> elementId=junction id, no contactPoint
wrong: Emitting more than one <successor> for a road
Using elementS/elementDir for ordinary road-road links

figures.caption: Figure 39. Types of elevation
figures.shows: Three panels. Road Elevation: a curve h(s) in the s-z plane, h measured vertically, local frame (s,t) moved along. Super Elevation: cross-section in the t-z plane; the road surface is rolled about the reference line (point s), h' is the rotated normal - elevation along t. Road Shape: cross-section with t positive to the LEFT; piecewise linear profile with widths 1 m, 4 m, 3 m, 1 m between t=5, 4, 0, -3, -4; h=0.05 m at t=5..4, h=0.45 m at t=0 (reference line peak), h=0 at t=-3..-4; slopes b=-0.10 m/m and b=0.15 m/m.
figures.lesson: Three independent height mechanisms: elevation (function of s), superelevation (roll angle about the reference line, function of s), shape (height offset as function of t, at given s). They add up.
right: Elevation for longitudinal grade from OSM/DEM
Superelevation for banking
Shape only for non-planar cross-sections (crown, crossfall)
wrong: Encoding crossfall as elevation or lane height
Treating shape t-axis as positive to the right - it is positive to the left as for all t

figures.caption: Figure 40. Superelevation
figures.shows: Cross-section in x-z with t pointing left. Left: a=0, road flat, a point at lateral distance t1 lies at horizontal distance t1. Right: a>0, road surface rotated about the reference point s so the left side rises; the point at t1 along the tilted surface projects horizontally to t1*cos(a); h axis is tilted with the surface.
figures.lesson: Superelevation is a pure rotation about the reference line: lane widths are measured along the tilted surface, so the plan-view footprint shrinks to t*cos(a) and the left edge rises by t*sin(a). Positive roll raises the left (positive t) side.
right: Measure lane widths along the rolled surface
Positive superelevation lifts the +t (left) side
wrong: Assuming plan-view (x,y) width stays equal to lane width under superelevation
Sign-flipping the roll angle (positive = right side down)
figures.formula: x_offset = t*cos(a); z = h_ref + t*sin(a); a(ds) = a + b*ds + c*ds^2 + d*ds^3 (radians)

figures.caption: Figure 41. Minimum t-definition range for road shapes
figures.shows: Plan view of a road (lanes 4..1 left, -1..-3 right) whose outer borders narrow along s. Two lateral profiles at s_R1 and s_R2 (red vertical lines); red circles mark the t-start of each shape polynomial: five at s_R1, three at s_R2, and each profile spans the full road width from outer left to outer right border (green bracket = minimum t range = maximum t extent of the whole road). A point (s_P, t_P) lies between the two profiles. Formulas: h_SR1(t_P) and h_SR2(t_P) = a + b*dt + c*dt^2 + d*dt^3, and h(s_P) printed as (h_SR1(t_P) + h_SR2(t_P))*(s_P - s_R1)/(s_R2 - s_R1).
figures.lesson: Each shape profile must cover the maximum t extent of the entire road, not only the local width; heights between profiles are interpolated linearly in s; within a profile, dt is measured from that polynomial's own t start.
right: Every s-profile covers t from the widest right edge to the widest left edge of the road
Linear interpolation along s between profiles
Profiles can have different numbers of polynomials
wrong: Defining shape only over the local road width - points elsewhere become undefined
Taking the printed formula literally: (h1+h2)*(sP-sR1)/(sR2-sR1) does not give h1 at sP=sR1; implement proper linear interpolation
figures.formula: h(s_P,t_P) = h_R1(t_P) + (h_R2(t_P) - h_R1(t_P))*(s_P - s_R1)/(s_R2 - s_R1); h_Ri(t) = a + b*dt + c*dt^2 + d*dt^3 with dt = t - t_start(polynomial). Figure prints (h_R1+h_R2)*(s_P-s_R1)/(s_R2-s_R1), which looks like a typo.

figures.caption: Figure 42. Shape definition (left) in combination with superelevation (right)
figures.shows: Same cross-section as Figure 40 but with a grey shape profile on top of the road (height rising toward +t). Left a=0: shape added vertically on a flat road. Right a>0: road rolled, the shape is applied perpendicular to the tilted surface (along tilted h), point t1 projects to t1*cos(a).
figures.lesson: Shape heights are applied in the superelevated (rolled) frame: shape is evaluated in t along the tilted surface and offset along the rolled h axis; superelevation is applied first, shape on top.
right: Compute shape in the local rolled frame
wrong: Adding shape height to global z after superelevation as if unrolled
figures.formula: p = ref + R(roll)*[t, h_shape(t)]

figures.caption: Figure 43. Road surface as defined in a CRG file
figures.shows: 3D rendering of a road surface with cobblestone (paving block) texture in one half and a smooth section with a pothole in the other, white dashed centre marking, kerbs on both sides - surface relief from a CRG file.
figures.lesson: OpenCRG supplies fine-grained surface relief (cobbles, potholes) on top of the OpenDRIVE road; it is not a substitute for lane geometry.
right: Reference CRG via <surface><CRG> only if real surface data exists
wrong: Trying to model surface relief with elevation/shape polynomials

figures.caption: Figure 44. ASAM OpenCRG road surface description using u/v-coordinates and x/y-coordinates
figures.shows: Plots of a sample CRG file (belgian block): XY overview of the CRG reference line (a curve from about (226,84) to (234,78)); XYZ height map in curved XY grid (z about 2.04-2.18 m); UVZ map in an uncurved grid, u = 730..740 m along the line, v = -1.5..1.5 m across.
figures.lesson: CRG has its own reference line and its own (u,v) coordinates, analogous to OpenDRIVE (s,t); combining requires a mapping between the two.
right: Treat u~s, v~t with offsets
wrong: Assuming CRG u starts at 0 or aligns with road s=0

figures.caption: Figure 45. Positioning of an ASAM OpenCRG file along the reference line
figures.shows: OpenDRIVE road in s/t (yellow +t, blue -t). A CRG grid placed from s_Start to s_End; the CRG reference line (black arrow) is offset below the road reference line by t_Offset.
figures.lesson: The CRG patch is valid only over [sStart, sEnd] and its reference line may be laterally shifted by tOffset relative to the road reference line.
right: Set sStart/sEnd to the CRG extent
wrong: Assuming the CRG reference line coincides with the road reference line
figures.formula: v = t - tOffset

figures.caption: Figure 46. ASAM OpenCRG attachment mode, attached
figures.shows: Mode attached: CRG grid with its u/v axes placed parallel to the road s/t axes, origin shifted by sOffset and tOffset; the CRG reference line is discarded and the patch bends with the OpenDRIVE reference line.
figures.lesson: In attached mode CRG (u,v) are simply (s - sOffset, t - tOffset); CRG heights are added to the OpenDRIVE height.
right: Use attached when surface detail should follow the OpenDRIVE geometry
wrong: Using CRG XY geometry in attached mode
figures.formula: u = s - sOffset; v = t - tOffset; z = crg(u,v)*zScale + zOffset + h_OpenDRIVE(s,t)

figures.caption: Figure 47. ASAM OpenCRG attached mode with elevation
figures.shows: Longitudinal profile: blue reference line elevation rising between sStart and sEnd; the CRG data (dark band) starts at sOffset and rides on top of the OpenDRIVE elevation.
figures.lesson: In attached mode the CRG relief is superimposed on the road elevation; heights outside the CRG data range are plain OpenDRIVE.
right: Total height = OpenDRIVE height + CRG delta
figures.formula: z_total = z_OpenDRIVE(s,t) + crg(u,v)*zScale + zOffset

figures.caption: Figure 48. ASAM OpenCRG attached0 mode with elevated reference line
figures.shows: Same profile in attached0 mode: OpenDRIVE elevation is set to zero (red line at z=0) inside [sStart,sEnd]; CRG data supplies the absolute height from sOffset; between the end of CRG data and sEnd there is a hatched region where height falls to z=0 - a gap.
figures.lesson: In attached0 the OpenDRIVE elevation is ignored, so sStart/sEnd must match the CRG data boundaries exactly or the surface drops to zero.
right: sStart/sEnd exactly equal to CRG data extent
wrong: sEnd beyond CRG data in attached0 - produces z=0 holes
figures.formula: z_total = crg(u,v)*zScale + zOffset (OpenDRIVE elevation := 0)

figures.caption: Figure 49. ASAM OpenCRG attachment mode, genuine
figures.shows: Mode genuine: CRG u/v axes rotated by hOffset relative to s/t and placed at (sOffset, tOffset); the CRG reference line (u) keeps its own curvature, not following s.
figures.lesson: In genuine mode the CRG geometry is used as-is relative to the start point (translated and rotated by hOffset); it does not bend with the OpenDRIVE reference line.
right: Use genuine for measured surfaces with their own geometry
wrong: Expecting genuine CRG to follow road curvature

figures.caption: Figure 50. ASAM OpenCRG orientation
figures.shows: Top: orientation=same, CRG grid corners A,B,C,D, origin (u=0,v=0) at sStart offset by tOffset, u along +s, v along +t. Bottom: orientation=opposite, grid rotated 180 deg (corner letters upside-down), u (labelled n) points to -s and v to -t; tOffset is shown on the other side.
figures.lesson: orientation=opposite is a 180 deg rotation about the CRG origin: both u and v reverse sign relative to s and t.
right: Flip both u and v for opposite
wrong: Flipping only u (mirror) - text matrix [[0,-1],[-1,0]] swaps axes; the figure shows a plain 180 deg rotation
figures.formula: opposite: u = -(s - sOffset), v = -(t - tOffset) (as drawn)

figures.section: 8.6.1 Modeling a road shape with a linear crossfall
figures.caption: Figure 51. Example crossfall modeled with road shape
figures.shows: Cross-section with t positive to the LEFT. Profile: flat h=0.05 m from t=5 to t=4 (width 1 m); slope down from h=0.45 m at t=0 to 0.05 at t=4 (width 4 m, b=-0.10 m/m); from h=0 at t=-3 rising to 0.45 at t=0 (width 3 m, b=0.15 m/m); flat h=0 from t=-4 to -3 (width 1 m). Table of four shape records all at s=0: t=4 a=0.05 b=0; t=0 a=0.45 b=-0.1; t=-3 a=0 b=0.15; t=-4 a=0 b=0.
figures.lesson: Each shape record is valid from its own t to the next larger t, and is evaluated with dt = t - t_record in the +t direction. Hence slope on the -t side is POSITIVE (0.15) because the profile rises towards the reference line when moving in +t.
right: Shape records sorted by t ascending at each s; dt measured from the record's t
One s value can hold several t-records forming a piecewise polynomial
wrong: Writing b with the visual slope sign (seen left-to-right in the drawing) - sign must refer to increasing t
Evaluating dt from t=0 instead of the record's t start
figures.formula: h(t) = a + b*(t - t_i) + c*(t - t_i)^2 + d*(t - t_i)^3 for t_i <= t < t_{i+1}

figures.caption: Figure 52. Center lane for road with lanes of different driving directions
figures.shows: Two-way road: lanes 3,2,1 above (yellow, left) and -1,-2 below (blue, right); centre lane 0 drawn as dash-dot line coinciding with the road reference line (no lane offset). At a vertical section boundary a new right lane -3 appears: the dashed boundary -1/-2 stays straight, a NEW dashed line peels off from it to the outer side and the solid outer edge swings outward, so the new lane opens with zero width next to lane -1; the old outer lane keeps its width and is now numbered -3 (labels -1, -2, -3 in the second part). Lane 3 on the left is separated by a solid line (e.g. shoulder).
figures.lesson: Lane ids are always contiguous from the centre lane (1,2,3 / -1,-2,-3) inside each lane section; when a lane is inserted the ids of all lanes outside it shift by one in the new section. Centre lane has no width; without laneOffset it equals the reference line.
right: Renumber lanes in each section consecutively from the centre
Link old -2 -> new -3, old -1 -> new -1; the new (zero-width-start) -2 has no predecessor
wrong: Keeping the old id for the continuing outer lane and giving the new lane id -3 when it is geometrically between -1 and the old -2
Linking the opening lane to old -2

figures.caption: Figure 53. Center lane for road with lanes of identical driving direction
figures.shows: One-way road: only left lanes 1, 2 (driving, arrows pointing AGAINST the reference line direction, i.e. leftwards) and 3 (separated by solid line), centre lane 0 on the reference line at the right edge of the road; no right lanes.
figures.lesson: A one-way road may consist of only one side; the centre lane then lies on the road edge. With right-hand traffic, left lanes are driven opposite to the reference line - so a one-way road built only of left lanes runs against s.
right: One-way: use only right lanes (traffic along +s in RHT), or only left lanes with traffic in -s
Centre lane at road edge is fine
wrong: Putting a one-way OSM way's lanes on the left side while expecting traffic in +s direction

figures.caption: Figure 54. UML model for lanes

figures.shows: Section A: lanes 1 | -1, ds1 starts at section A start; lane -1 constant width (a=const, b=c=d=0). figures.caption: Figure 77. Types of roads in a junction (right-hand traffic)
figures.shows: Five-arm junction inside a dashed pentagon 'junction area'. Blue arrows are road reference lines; red curves are connecting roads. NW arm: two-way road (lanes -1 / 1), reference line points INTO the junction (road ends there) - labelled incoming road. NE arm: one-way road with lanes -2,-1 on the right of a reference line pointing into the junction - incoming road (one-way). W arm: two-way (-1/1), reference line points AWAY (road starts at junction) - still an incoming road. S arm: two-way (1/-1), reference line points into junction - incoming road. E arm: one-way road with lanes 1,2 (yellow, left side), reference line pointing east away from junction, labelled 'Not an incoming road (one-way street)'. Connecting roads fan out from every incoming arm to the reachable arms; none start on the E arm. Note: as drawn, left lanes 1,2 in RHT would carry traffic toward the junction; the label (outgoing-only one-way) is the intended meaning, so the lane colouring looks inconsistent.

Keep all connecting roads within one junction area polygon

Creating connecting roads that start on an outgoing-only arm

figures.caption: Figure 78. UML model for junctions
figures.shows: UML of t_junction (id, mainRoad[0..1], name[0..1], orientation[0..1], sEnd[0..1], sStart[0..1], type e_junction_type[0..1]). Children: connection 1..* (t_junction_connection: connectingRoad[0..1], contactPoint[0..1], id, incomingRoad[0..1], linkedRoad[0..1], type e_connection_type[0..1]) which has predecessor 0..1 / successor 0..1 (t_junction_predecessorSuccessor: elementDir, elementId, elementS, elementType='road') and laneLink 0..* (from:int, to:int); priority 0..* (high, low); controller 0..* (id, sequence[0..1], type[0..1]); surface 0..1 with CRG 0..* (file, mode=global, purpose[0..1], zOffset[0..1], zScale[0..1]).

figures.caption: Figure 79. Connecting roads of junction with id 1 (left hand traffic)
figures.shows: Four-arm signalised X junction in LEFT-hand traffic with 3 lanes per direction. Each arm has lanes 1,2,3 on one side and -1,-2,-3 on the other, stop lines and turn arrows, one traffic light per approach. Road 28 pred road 4 (start) succ road 2 (start); road 61 pred road 4 (start) succ road 3 (end); road 64 pred road 4 (start) succ road 1 (start). Lane links: 28:1 pred -3 succ 3; 61:1 pred -2 succ -2; 61:2 pred -3 succ -3; 64:1 pred -1 succ 1. Incoming roads carry no lane links to junction lanes.

figures.caption: Figure 80. Direct junctions
figures.shows: Road 1 (lanes 1, -1..-4) ends at a vertical black cut line. After the cut, road 2 (lanes 1, -1..-3) continues straight and road 3 (single lane -1) bends away to the lower right, continuing lane -4 of road 1. All reference lines point to the right; road 3's reference line starts at the outer edge of road 2's lane -3 at the cut. No lane overlaps. wrong: Inserting a connecting road for a simple split

Using connectingRoad attribute in a direct junction

figures.caption: Figure 81. Cases when direct junctions cannot be modeled

figures.caption: Figure 82. Example of a virtual junction showing a parking lot entry and exit

figures.caption: Figure 83. Virtual junction with virtual connections

figures.caption: Figure 84. Junction group with three junctions

figures.shows: UML: t_junctionGroup (id, name[0..1], type e_junctionGroup_type) with junctionReference 1..* (junction: string). e_junctionGroup_type = roundabout | unknown.
figures.lesson: A junctionGroup must reference at least one junction and needs a type.
right: Always write type (roundabout or unknown) and >=1 junctionReference
wrong: Empty junctionGroup
Referencing non-existent junction ids

figures.caption: Figure 86. X-Junction with four traffic lights and two controllers
figures.shows: X junction (RHT) with a traffic light at each of the four corners, each just before its approach's stop line. Controller id=1 points to the NW light (serving southbound traffic, seen from behind) and the SE light (serving northbound, shown green): the opposing N/S approaches. Controller id=2 points to the NE and SW lights (E/W approaches), both shown red.
figures.lesson: Signals that always show the same state (opposing approaches of one phase) belong to one controller; the junction lists its controllers (with optional sequence priority) so an OpenSCENARIO tool can switch phases.
right: Group opposing approaches' lights into one <controller> with one <control signalId=..> per light
Reference each controller from <junction><controller id= sequence=>
wrong: One controller per light (loses phase coupling)
Putting conflicting approaches in the same controller

figures.caption: Figure 87. UML model for controller
figures.shows: UML: t_controller (id, name[0..1], sequence nonNegativeInteger[0..1]) with control 1..* (signalId: string, type: string[0..1]).
figures.lesson: A top-level controller must control at least one signal.
right: Emit <controller> under <OpenDRIVE> with >=1 <control signalId>
wrong: Controller without control children
signalId pointing to a non-dynamic or missing signal

figures.caption: Figure 88. A circular and angular object
figures.shows: Road with reference line along the top (s right, t up), lanes -1,-2,-3 below. A circular object (centre M) at (s1, t1) beside lane -3 with radius r. An angular (rectangular) object at (s2, t2) inside lane -3, with its local u axis along s and v axis along t; 'length' is drawn along u and 'width' along v. t is measured from the reference line (negative to the right).
figures.lesson: Objects are placed by (s, t, zOffset) of their origin (centre of bounding box) in road coordinates; shape is either radius (circular) or length+width (angular), plus height. Figure draws length along u, but the 1.7 attribute table says length is along v and width along u - an internal inconsistency to be aware of.
right: Place object origin at bounding-box centre via s/t
Use radius XOR length/width, never both
Use hdg relative to road direction for rotated rectangles
wrong: Giving both radius and length/width
Placing by corner instead of centre

figures.caption: Figure 89. UML model for objects
figures.shows: UML of t_road_objects with children object 0..*, objectReference 0..*, tunnel 0..*, bridge 0..*. t_road_objects_object attributes: dynamic, hdg, height, id, length, name, orientation, perpToRoad, pitch, radius, roll, s, subtype, t, type, validLength, width, zOffset; children repeat 0..*, material 0..*, validity 0..*, parkingSpace 0..1, markings 0..1 (marking 1..*, cornerReference 2..*), borders 0..1 (border 1..*: outlineId, type, useCompleteOutline, width), outline 0..1 (legacy) and outlines 0..1 (outline 1..*: closed, fillType, id, laneType, outer) each with cornerRoad 0..* (dz, height, id, s, t) or cornerLocal 0..* (height, id, u, v, z), surface 0..1 (CRG: file, hideRoadSurfaceCRG, zScale).
figures.lesson: Structure reference for writing objects: outlines wrap outline; cornerRoad and cornerLocal are alternatives; markings reference outline corner ids.
right: Write s, t, zOffset, id, type on every object
Use <outlines><outline id=..> (not the legacy single <outline>) for new files
wrong: Mixing cornerRoad and cornerLocal in one outline
Omitting required s/t/zOffset

figures.caption: Figure 90. Placing objects on roads
figures.shows: Side view (z vs s): a blue road elevation profile that is flat then rises steeply. A long grey flat object is placed at an insertion point on the curve; it cuts into the rising road surface on one end and floats above it at the other.
figures.lesson: Objects are rigid and do not follow elevation/superelevation; on roads with elevation or lateral profiles they must be small enough not to intersect or float noticeably. Long objects must be split or made repeated (repeat follows the road).
right: Use <repeat> (continuous, distance=0) for long linear features like guard rails, walls
Keep single objects short on graded roads; set perpToRoad only for objects smaller than the elevation curvature radius
wrong: Placing one long rigid object along a hill
Ignoring zOffset relative to the reference line elevation

figures.caption: Figure 91. One larger angular repeated object
figures.shows: Top view: a curved road (lanes -1, -2) and a blue continuous strip beside lane -2 starting at s, extending 'length' along the reference line. Labelled tStart and widthStart at the start, tEnd and widthEnd at the end (lateral offset and width change along the strip). Side view: strip with heightStart / zOffsetStart at the start and heightEnd / zOffsetEnd at the end (height shrinks, zOffset grows).
figures.lesson: A repeat with distance=0 is a continuous object (guard rail, wall, noise barrier) whose t, width, height and zOffset are interpolated linearly from Start to End over the repeat length, following the road curvature.
right: Model OSM barrier=guard_rail/wall/fence along a road as one object with <repeat distance=0>
Use tStart/tEnd to follow the road edge when road width changes
wrong: Writing hundreds of small objects for a continuous barrier
Assuming repeat length is in object-local units (it is along the reference line in s)
figures.formula: value(s) = valueStart + (valueEnd - valueStart) * (s - sRepeat) / length  for t, width, height, zOffset

figures.caption: Figure 92. Several smaller angular repeated objects
figures.shows: Top view: same curved road; discrete blue rectangles are repeated every 'distance' along s starting at s; their centres follow a dash-dot line from tStart to tEnd; size shrinks from widthStart/lengthStart to widthEnd/lengthEnd, and each rectangle is rotated to the local road heading. Side view: heights from heightStart to heightEnd, zOffset from zOffsetStart to zOffsetEnd.
figures.lesson: A repeat with distance>0 yields discrete instances at s + k*distance; each instance is oriented with the road and parameters are interpolated.
right: Use repeat distance>0 for posts, street lamps, bollards, trees in rows
Expect instance orientation to follow road heading
wrong: Setting distance larger than length and expecting more than one instance
figures.formula: s_k = s + k*distance, k = 0..floor(length/distance); params interpolated linearly in s

figures.caption: Figure 93. Several smaller circular repeated objects
figures.shows: As Figure 92 but with circles shrinking from radiusStart to radiusEnd; side view shows heights shrinking and zOffset rising from zOffsetStart to zOffsetEnd.
figures.lesson: Circular objects repeat with radiusStart/radiusEnd instead of width/length.
right: Use radiusStart/radiusEnd for round repeated objects (trees, bollards)
wrong: Mixing radius and width/length on one repeat

figures.caption: Figure 94. Traffic island as object
figures.shows: Road with lanes 3,2 above and -2,-3 below the reference line (s to the right); lane 2 traffic flows left, lane -2 to the right. Around the reference line the inner lanes widen into a lens shape with white hatched (chevron) markings, and in the middle sits a grey rounded-rectangle traffic island lying on the reference line.
figures.lesson: A traffic island inside a road is an object (type trafficIsland) with an outline, placed in a region where the inner lanes (typically restricted/median type, widening from zero) open up; hatching is object marking or road marks. Multiple outlines may describe island body, curb border and pedestrian refuge.
right: Model OSM traffic islands as object type=trafficIsland with closed outline + border type=curb
Widen inner (median/restricted) lanes around the island so driving lanes are pushed outward rather than overlapping the island
wrong: Placing an island object on top of driving lanes without lane widening

figures.caption: Figure 95. An object described by corner road coordinates
figures.shows: Inertial X/Y grid with an S-shaped road from (10,10) to (45,55); s ticks every 10 m from 0 to 80 with perpendicular dashed lines; t axis shown at s=0. Next to it, a 9-corner polygon with corners [s1,t1]..[s9,t9] (counter-clockwise from left: s1,t1 left, s2,t2 bottom, ... s8,t8 top-left, s9,t9 notch).
figures.lesson: cornerRoad corners are given in road coordinates (s, t, dz, height); the outline therefore bends with the road. Points of an area outline should be listed counter-clockwise.
right: Use cornerRoad for objects that hug a road (barriers, islands, crosswalks)
Order area corners counter-clockwise
At least two cornerRoad points per outline
wrong: Mixing cornerRoad with cornerLocal in one outline
Clockwise area outlines

figures.caption: Figure 96. An object described by corner local coordinates
figures.shows: Road from (15,70) curving up; s marks 0..50. A green arrow goes from the road at s=20 to point P (object origin) at s=20, t=-30, zOffset=0, hdg=7pi/4 rad. At P a local u/v frame is rotated by hdg; the same 9-corner polygon is now given in [u1,v1]..[u9,v9].
figures.lesson: cornerLocal corners are given in the object's local u/v frame whose origin is (s,t,zOffset) of the object and whose rotation is hdg relative to the road; the outline is rigid (does not bend with the road).
right: Use cornerLocal for buildings, rigid islands, parking lots referenced to one point
Rotate local u/v by road heading at s plus hdg
wrong: Interpreting u/v as inertial axes
Forgetting hdg is relative to road direction
figures.formula: x = x_road(s,t) + u*cos(theta) - v*sin(theta); y = y_road(s,t) + u*sin(theta) + v*cos(theta); theta = heading_road(s) + hdg

figures.caption: Figure 97. Parking spaces rectangular (left figure) and rhomboid (right figure)
figures.shows: Left: road with reference line on top, lanes -1, -2 and a parking strip below; three green rectangular parking spaces with origins at (s1,t1), (s2,t2), (s3,t3), aligned with s. Right: same, but the spaces are rotated (angled parking) about their origins.
figures.lesson: Each parking space is an object type=parkingSpace placed by s/t (and hdg for angled bays), optionally with outline and a <parkingSpace access=...> child.
right: Emit one parkingSpace object per bay, or a repeated object for regular rows
Use hdg for angled/rhomboid bays
wrong: Modelling parking bays as driving lanes

figures.caption: Figure 98. Crosswalk in ASAM OpenDRIVE
figures.shows: Two-lane road (lane 1 above, lane -1 below the reference line, each t=3.50 m wide). A trapezoidal crosswalk outline: top corners at s1=5.00 and s4=15.00 (t=+3.5), bottom corners at s2=8.00 and s3=12.00 (t=-3.5). The slanted sides carry dashed white/grey markings. Spec XML: object type=crosswalk id=10 s=10 t=0 length=10 width=7 orientation=none, outline cornerRoad (5,3.5),(8,-3.5),(12,-3.5),(15,3.5), two <marking> elements referencing corners 0-1 and 2-3 (width 0.1, white, lineLength 0.2, spaceLength 0.05, zOffset 0.005).
figures.lesson: A crosswalk is an object of type crosswalk spanning the road width with a cornerRoad outline; its edge lines are object markings referencing outline corner ids. It is valid in both directions (orientation=none).
right: Model OSM highway=crossing on a road as object type=crosswalk with cornerRoad outline covering all lanes
Add <markings> with cornerReference pairs for the edge lines; color must be set
Use orientation=none
If the crossing spans several roads, define it once and add <objectReference> on the others
wrong: Modelling a plain crosswalk as a signal (only binding traffic signs/marks are signals)
Marking without color
cornerReference without an outline

figures.caption: Figure 99. A tunnel
figures.shows: Road with lanes 3,2,1 (traffic to the left) and -1,-2 (traffic to the right); a semi-transparent grey box labelled tunnel covers the full cross section over an s range.
figures.lesson: A tunnel is a <tunnel s= length= type= > element (not an <object>), valid for the whole cross section unless restricted by validity.
right: Emit <tunnel> for OSM tunnel=yes segments with s/length on the road
Always set @type (standard|underpass)
wrong: Modelling a tunnel as <object type=...>
Missing tunnel type

figures.caption: Figure 100. A bridge
figures.shows: Same road layout; a grey box labelled bridge spans the full cross section over a shorter s range.
figures.lesson: A bridge is a <bridge s= length= type= > element valid for the whole cross section unless restricted.
right: Emit <bridge> for OSM bridge=yes segments with type concrete|steel|wood|brick
wrong: Omitting bridge type
Using an object for the bridge deck

figures.caption: Figure 101. CRG for Objects
figures.shows: Curved road reference line (s). A green t vector leads from the reference line to the centre of a rotated, chequered CRG patch; the CRG u/v axes are aligned with the object's local frame and the origin (0|0)CRG is the object centre.
figures.lesson: Object CRG uses the object's local u/v frame (origin at object centre, so u/v are positive and negative); the CRG reference line is ignored.
right: Only attach <surface><CRG> to angular objects (length/width), not circular or outlined ones
wrong: Using the CRG file's own reference line or inertial position
figures.formula: objectSurfaceHeight(u,v) = crgEvaluv2z(crg,u,v) * zScale

figures.section: 11.11 Object surface - Table 73 Total height calculation by attachment mode
figures.caption: (no caption) road surface CRG mode=attached, hideRoadSurfaceCRG=true
figures.shows: Side view: road elevation curve (blue) with a stepped road-surface CRG profile riding on it from sStart to sEnd; inside the object's extent the road CRG is replaced by a flat-topped object CRG block sitting on the OpenDRIVE elevation.
figures.lesson: Total height under an object CRG depends on the road surface CRG mode and hideRoadSurfaceCRG: OpenDRIVE height + object CRG. Where crgEvaluv2z returns NaN the object has no effect.
right: Set hideRoadSurfaceCRG=false whenever an overlapping road CRG is not mode=attached
Ignore object @height/@zOffset for surface elevation when <surface> is present
wrong: hideRoadSurfaceCRG=true over attached0/genuine/global road CRG

right: Set hideRoadSurfaceCRG=false whenever an overlapping road CRG is not mode=attached
Ignore object @height/@zOffset for surface elevation when <surface> is present
wrong: hideRoadSurfaceCRG=true over attached0/genuine/global road CRG

figures.shows: Road elevation rises, but the road-surface CRG data stays near z=0 (absolute/genuine data not following the OpenDRIVE elevation); the object block sits on it.

Ignore object @height/@zOffset for surface elevation when <surface> is present

right: Set hideRoadSurfaceCRG=false whenever an overlapping road CRG is not mode=attached
Ignore object @height/@zOffset for surface elevation when <surface> is present

figures.section: 11.11 Object surface - Table 73 Total height calculation by attachment mode
