figures.caption: UML class diagram 'Link'
figures.shows: t_road_link -> predecessor 0..1, successor 0..1 of t_road_link_predecessorSuccessor: elementId, elementType (road|junction), contactPoint[0..1], elementS[0..1], elementDir[0..1].
figures.lesson: Road links point to a road (with contactPoint) or a junction; elementS/elementDir allow linking into the middle of a road (virtual junction context).
right: contactPoint mandatory when elementType=road
Omit contactPoint for junction links
wrong: contactPoint on a junction link
figures.new: Unchanged in essence; elementS/elementDir exist since 1.6.

figures.caption: UML class diagram 'Lanes'
figures.shows: t_road_lanes: layer [0..1]=permanent; constraints: permanent layer laneSections have no @length; if laneOffset exists no lane may use border. laneOffset 0..* (s,a,b,c,d); laneSection 1..* (s, length[0..1], singleSide[0..1]) -> center 1 (lane 1, id=0, type/level deprecated), left 0..1 (lane 1..*, id positive), right 0..1 (lane 1..*, id negative). Lane (t_road_lanes_laneSection_lr_lane): type, advisory=none, direction=standard, dynamicLaneType, dynamicLaneDirection, level, roadWorks=false; link 0..1 -> predecessor/successor 0..* (id, layer=permanent); choice width 1..* xor border 1..*; roadMark 0..*; height 0..* (sOffset, inner, outer); rule 0..* (sOffset, value); material 0..*; speed 0..* (sOffset, max, unit); access 0..* (sOffset, rule allow/deny, restriction deprecated) -> restriction 0..* (type).
figures.lesson: Lane model for writing: width polynomials (not border when laneOffset present), multiple predecessors/successors allowed (lane splits), lane access with nested restriction children, direction/advisory attributes, center lane type deprecated.
right: Use width (not border)
Write access as <access sOffset rule='allow'><restriction type='bus'/></access>
Allow multiple successor ids at lane splits
wrong: border lanes together with laneOffset
Using deprecated access@restriction attribute
Setting type on the center lane
figures.new: advisory, direction, dynamicLane*, roadWorks, link layer, nested access restriction are post-1.7 additions.

figures.caption: UML class diagram 'RoadMark'
figures.shows: t_road_lanes_laneSection_lcr_lane_roadMark: sOffset, type, weight[0..1], color, material[0..1], width[0..1], laneChange[0..1], height[0..1]; sway 0..* (ds,a,b,c,d), type 0..1 (name, width) -> line 1..* (length, space, tOffset, sOffset, rule, width, color), explicit 0..1 -> line 1..* (length, tOffset, sOffset, rule, width).
figures.lesson: Lane boundary markings; complex patterns via type/line; explicit lines for surveyed dashes.
right: color is required
Use laneChange to express crossing permission
wrong: Using lane roadMarks for stop lines or crosswalks (those are objects/signals)
figures.new: Unchanged structure vs 1.7 apart from minor attribute types.

figures.caption: UML class diagram 'Junction'
figures.shows: Abstract t_junction (name[0..1], id) with planView 0..1 (junction reference line), surface 0..1, elevationGrid 0..1, boundary 0..1, objects 0..1, controller 0..* (id, type, sequence), priority 0..* (high, low), crossPath 0..* (crossingRoad, id, roadAtStart, roadAtEnd; startLaneLink/endLaneLink 1 each: s, from, to). Subclasses: t_junction_common (type default; connection 0..* of t_junction_connection_common: connectingRoad), t_junction_direct (connection 1..* with linkedRoad), t_junction_virtual (mainRoad, sStart, sEnd, orientation; connection_virtual (deprecated, with predecessor/successor) xor connection_virtual_default), t_junction_crossing (roadSection 1..*: id, roadId, sStart, sEnd). Base t_junction_connection: id, incomingRoad[0..1], contactPoint[0..1]; laneLink 0..* (from, to, overlapZone[0..1], fromLayer, toLayer).
figures.lesson: Junctions can carry their own <objects> (e.g. crosswalks attached to the junction reference line) and controllers; pedestrian crossings are crossPaths; crossing junction type models road/rail crossings.
right: Attach junction-wide objects (crosswalks, stop lines spanning several connecting roads) to the junction <objects> with a junction planView
Reference controllers from the junction
Use crossPath for pedestrian crossings inside junctions
wrong: Using deprecated virtual connection predecessor/successor
figures.new: Junction-level planView/objects/boundary/elevationGrid/crossPath and crossing type are new since 1.8.

figures.caption: UML class diagram 'JunctionBoundary'
figures.shows: t_junction_boundary -> segment 1..* (abstract, roadId) specialised as segment_lane (type lane, boundaryLane, sStart, sEnd as grEqZero or contactPoint) and segment_joint (type joint, contactPoint, jointLaneStart[0..1], jointLaneEnd[0..1], transitionLength[0..1]).
figures.lesson: The junction area outline is built from lane segments along connecting roads and joint segments across road ends.
right: Alternate lane and joint segments to close the boundary
figures.new: New since 1.8.

figures.caption: UML class diagram 'ElevationGrid'
figures.shows: t_junction_elevationGrid (sStart, gridSpacing) -> elevation 0..* (left[0..1], center, right[0..1] as space-separated double lists t_junction_grid_position_list).
figures.lesson: Junction surface height sampled on a grid along the junction reference line.
right: Use gridSpacing consistent with junction planView length
figures.new: New since 1.8.

figures.caption: UML class diagram 'JunctionGroup'
figures.shows: t_junctionGroup (name[0..1], id, type e_junctionGroup_type) -> junctionReference 1..* (junction).
figures.lesson: Groups junctions (e.g. roundabout) at top level.
right: At least one junctionReference
figures.new: Same as 1.7 Figure 85.

figures.caption: Figure 1. Complex junction
figures.shows: Real-world style top view of a signalised 5-arm junction: N arm two-way with a curb-side BUS lane (southbound) and a painted/raised teardrop splitter island between the inbound and outbound halves; E arm two-way with left/straight turn arrows and a stop line set back from a zebra; W arm two-way inbound with two eastbound arrows and a stop line; SW arm one-way inbound (northbound) with straight, right-turn and a dashed BUS+bicycle lane; SE arm one-way outbound (blue one-way arrow sign pointing away, red no-entry disk at the corner). Zebra crossings sit just inside every arm mouth. Vehicle signals (3-aspect, arrow aspects, white-bar tram/bus aspects), pedestrian signals at both crossing ends, give-way triangles and mandatory-direction signs are drawn once per approach.
figures.lesson: A single real junction mixes one-way in/out arms, bus/bike lanes, splitter islands, zebras and many signal kinds; the guideline builds it up from T to X to the full 5-road case.
right: Treat the whole mouth area (all arms up to and including the zebras) as one common junction.
Represent duplicated real signal heads only where needed; the figure shows one head per approach/crossing.
wrong: Splitting the 5-arm node into several small junctions just because the arms are skewed.
Dropping one-way arms or bus/bike lanes from the junction model.

figures.caption: Figure 2. Basic T junction
figures.shows: T junction: a two-lane two-way road enters from the W, a two-way road from the ENE and a two-way road from the S. The priority road bends between E and S (yellow priority diamonds with the supplementary bent-priority plate on the E and S approaches), shown by a dashed white guide line curving from the E arm into the S arm through the junction. The W approach has a give-way triangle with the same bent-priority plate. Dark grey bands outside thin white edge lines are curb+sidewalk on all arms; inner corners are rounded curbs.
figures.lesson: Priority in a T can follow a bent through-route; priority is expressed with traffic signs, and the dashed guide marking belongs to the connecting road of the priority movement.
right: Keep curb + sidewalk running continuously around every corner of the junction.
Model the priority route with priority signs on the main arms and a yield sign on the minor arm.
wrong: Assuming the geometrically straight pair (W-E) is the priority road.
Ending sidewalks at the junction boundary.

figures.caption: Figure 3. Road reference lines
figures.shows: Blue arrows on the road centre lines: road 4 (W) runs W->E and ends at the W mouth of the junction; road 6 (E) runs E->W and ends at the E mouth; road 5 (S) starts at the S mouth and runs southward. All three reference lines stop exactly where the curb returns begin (the gore points), nothing of them lies inside the junction area.
figures.lesson: Reference lines of the arm roads end/start at the junction outline (the curb-return tangent points), and their direction is free: a road may start or end at the junction.
right: Cut each OSM way at the junction outline and let its reference line start or end there.
Allow either direction (road may end or start at the junction); record the correct contactPoint.
wrong: Running an arm reference line into the junction centre (the OSM node).
Reversing ways just to make all of them point into the junction.

figures.caption: Figure 4. Lanes on the road with @id="4"
figures.shows: Road 4 coloured by lane: lane 1 (beige, left of reference line) and lane -1 (light blue, right) are driving lanes; at each outer edge a thin violet strip (curb) and a dark-red band (walking/sidewalk). Code 2: left 3 walking, 2 curb, 1 driving; right -1 driving, -2 curb, -3 walking, level=false.
figures.lesson: Standard urban cross-section per side: driving, then a narrow curb lane, then a walking lane, ids counted outward from the centre lane.
right: Per side: driving lanes, then type curb (~0.15 m), then type walking.
Number lanes outward from 0: left positive, right negative.
wrong: Modelling sidewalks as separate roads parallel to the carriageway when they are attached to it.
Omitting the curb lane between driving and walking lanes.

figures.caption: Figure 5. Lanes on all roads
figures.shows: All three arms with the same cross-section. Road 6 (reference line pointing W into the junction) has -1 on its N side and 1 on its S side; road 5 (reference line pointing S, starting at junction) has -1 on the W side and 1 on the E side. The junction interior is still unmodelled grey.
figures.lesson: Lane ids follow each road's own reference-line direction, so the same physical side can be +1 on one arm and -1 on another.
right: Derive lane ids per road from its s-direction, not from compass side.
wrong: Assuming lane -1 always means the inbound lane of a junction arm.

figures.caption: Figure 6. Junction area between the roads
figures.shows: Red outline = junction 10: straight cut lines across the full road width (including curbs and sidewalks) at the three road ends, joined by the outer curb lines; the inner corners follow the rounded curb returns (W-S corner is a tight rounded return, S-E corner a long sweeping curve), the N side is the straight continuation of the north sidewalk.
figures.lesson: The junction area is the polygon bounded by the arm end cuts and the curb/sidewalk outer edges; it contains the sidewalk corners too. Keep it as small as possible but as big as needed.
right: Cut each arm perpendicular to its reference line across the full width incl. sidewalks.
Close the polygon along the outer edges of the corner sidewalks/curbs.
wrong: A junction polygon that only covers the carriageway and leaves sidewalk corners unassigned.
An oversized junction that swallows long stretches of the arms.

figures.caption: Figure 7. Connecting roads
figures.shows: Inside the red outline three blue connecting-road reference lines: road 46 straight from end of road 4 to end of road 6; road 45 curving right from end of road 4 to start of road 5; road 56 curving from start of road 5 to end of road 6. Each connecting road starts and ends exactly at the arm reference-line end points.
figures.lesson: One connecting road per pair of arms (per path), its reference line continuous in position and heading with the arm reference lines at both ends; connecting roads may overlap each other.
right: Start/end every connecting road at the arm reference-line endpoint with matching heading (G1).
Use predecessor/successor with contactPoint start/end matching where the arm road begins or ends.
wrong: Connecting roads that start at lane centres instead of the arm reference line without a laneOffset.
A kink in heading where the connecting road meets the arm.

figures.caption: Figure 8. Connecting road with @id="46" and its lanes
figures.shows: Connecting road 46 (straight W->E along the N side) carries lane 1 (beige) and -1 (blue) driving lanes, and on its left (north) side curb lane 2 and walking lane 3 which continue the north curb+sidewalk of roads 4 and 6 straight through the junction. Its right (south) side has no curb/sidewalk because that side faces the open junction interior.
figures.lesson: Curbs and sidewalks are carried THROUGH the junction on the connecting roads that run along the junction edge; sides facing the interior get only driving lanes.
right: Give boundary connecting roads curb+walking lanes on the side that follows the junction outline.
Give interior-facing sides only the driving lanes.
wrong: Breaking the sidewalk at the junction boundary.
Adding curb/sidewalk lanes on interior sides of connecting roads where they would overlap other paths.

figures.caption: Figure 9. Lane links for lanes with @type="driving"
figures.shows: Six red arrows inside the junction, one per permitted driving movement: 4->6 straight, 6->4 straight, 4->5 right turn, 5->4 left turn, 5->6 right turn, 6->5 left turn. Each arrow runs from the inbound lane of one arm to the outbound lane of another.
figures.lesson: Every permitted movement needs a lane link from the inbound lane of the incoming road to the matching connecting-road lane; two-way connecting roads serve both directions.
right: Create one laneLink per permitted (incoming lane -> connecting lane) relation, for both directions of travel.
Also link curb and walking lanes where the connecting road carries them (Code 7).
wrong: Linking only one direction of a two-way connecting road.
Linking outbound lanes of an arm as 'from' lanes.

figures.caption: Figure 10. Traffic signs for priority
figures.shows: Lane-coloured T junction with the red junction outline, the three connecting reference lines and signs: priority-road diamond + bent-priority plate at the E and S arms, yield triangle + bent-priority plate on the W arm just before the junction (road 4, s=68 near its end, t=-4 on the right side).
figures.lesson: Priority is set with sign signals on the incoming roads at their junction end, valid for the inbound lane; the sign can carry semantics priority type=yield.
right: Place the priority/yield sign as a signal on the incoming road near the junction with validity on the inbound lane(s).
Add semantics (priority yield) for machine-readable priority.
wrong: Placing approach signs on the connecting roads inside the junction.
Omitting lane validity so the sign applies to the opposite direction too.

figures.caption: Figure 11. Complete basic T junction
figures.shows: Final basic T: all arms with lane colours, junction outline, white road-end bars, grey edge lines continuing as curves through the junction along the curb returns, a dashed grey guide line through the junction on the priority bend (E->S) and dashed centre lines on the arms; yield triangle on W, priority diamonds on E and S.
figures.lesson: Road marks complete the junction: broken centre line on the arms, edge lines continued along the connecting roads, guide line for the priority route on its connecting road.
right: Put centre-line roadMark (broken, laneChange both) on lane 0 of the arms.
Continue edge lines through the junction on the connecting roads that follow the curbs.
wrong: Drawing every connecting road's markings (would clutter the interior).
No edge markings inside the junction.

figures.caption: Figure 12. Lowered sidewalk
figures.shows: 3D render: zebra crossing meets a curb that is fully lowered over the crossing width with short ramps at both ends; behind it the sidewalk is lowered only on its curb side (sloping up to full height on the grass side); lamp post on the grass.
figures.lesson: Lowered curbs and sidewalks at crossings are modelled with lane <height> records (inner/outer) on the curb and walking lanes, not with geometry changes.
right: Curb lane: height 0.12 -> 0.02 over 0.5 m, hold 0.02 over the crossing, back to 0.12 (Code 11).
Walking lane: lower only the inner (curb) edge to 0.02, keep outer at 0.12 (Code 12).
wrong: Cutting the curb lane (width 0) at the crossing.
Lowering the whole sidewalk width.

figures.caption: Figure 13. Advanced T junction
figures.shows: Same T as Fig. 2 plus signals: on each approach a stop line across the inbound lane, a vehicle signal on a mast arm over the lane and one at the roadside; pedestrian crossings on all three arms just inside the junction mouth (W arm marked by two dotted lines, E and S arms as zebras), with pedestrian signals at both ends of every crossing. Priority signs remain.
figures.lesson: Signalised T: stop lines on the incoming roads, vehicle lights and controllers, pedestrian crossings with their own stop lines, lights and controllers.
right: Model each approach: stop line + one or more lights + controller.
Model each crossing as its own walking road with invisible stop lines and pedestrian lights.
wrong: Treating the zebra only as a road mark with no crossing road / crossPath.

figures.caption: Figure 14. Traffic lights and stop lines
figures.shows: Lane-coloured T with the red outline: grey stop-line bars on the inbound lane of each arm just outside the junction outline; for each approach two signal heads (one on a mast arm above the lane, one at the roadside) placed just inside the junction at the start of the connecting roads; priority signs kept.
figures.lesson: Stop lines live on the incoming road; traffic lights are placed at their physical location, which may be on a connecting road inside the junction (s=2.5 of road 46).
right: Put the stop line on the incoming road near its junction end with lane validity.
Put the light on whatever road it physically stands at; link it by <reference> to the stop line.
wrong: Moving the light onto the incoming road just to sit next to the stop line.
Giving the traffic light its own lane validity.

figures.caption: Figure 15. Pedestrian crossings
figures.shows: Three crossing roads (hatched dark-red walking areas with blue reference lines across the carriageway) placed just inside the junction outline on the W, E and S arms, beyond the stop lines. Each reference line runs from the sidewalk on one side of the arm to the sidewalk on the other side.
figures.lesson: Pedestrian crossings inside a common junction are extra roads of that junction (junction=id) carrying one walking lane, and are tied to the sidewalks via crossPath.
right: Create the crosswalk road inside the junction, just after the stop line, spanning sidewalk to sidewalk.
Set its junction attribute to the junction id.
wrong: Placing the crossing road outside the junction on the arm when it lies within the junction mouth.
Linking crossing roads with connections/laneLinks instead of crossPath.

figures.caption: Figure 16. Details of the stop lines and traffic lights
figures.shows: Close-up at the W mouth: road 4 reference line ends, roads 46 (straight) and 45 (right turn) begin; stop line 1 across road 4's inbound lane; traffic light 4 on a mast arm over the lane and light 2 at the roadside, both at the start of road 46; crossing road 75 runs N->S across the mouth (dotted edges); pedestrian light 9 + invisible stop line 20 at its N end, invisible stop line 21 + pedestrian light 3 at its S end.
figures.lesson: Shows the id wiring: lights 2/4 reference stop line 1; stop line 1 depends on lights 2 and 4; pedestrian lights on road 75 reference the invisible stop line at the opposite end of the crossing.
right: Pedestrian waiting positions are invisible stop lines (type 11000001, semantics waitingLine) on the crossing road.
A pedestrian light on one kerb controls pedestrians waiting at the other kerb (it faces them).
wrong: Referencing the stop line on the same side as the pedestrian light by default.

figures.caption: Figure 17. Details of a pedestrian crossing
figures.shows: Lane ids at the W mouth: road 4 lanes 3,2,1 | 0 | -1,-2,-3; road 46 (straight, along N edge) lanes 3,2,1,0,-1; road 45 (right turn) lanes 1,0,-1,-2,-3 with curb -2 and walking -3 hugging the inner corner. Crossing road 75 (single walking lane 1) spans from road 46's walking lane 3 (north sidewalk) to road 45's walking lane -3 (corner sidewalk).
figures.lesson: crossPath links the crossing road to the sidewalk lanes OF THE CONNECTING ROADS (roadAtStart=46 lane 3, roadAtEnd=45 lane -3), which proves sidewalks run on connecting roads inside the junction.
right: Carry corner sidewalks on the turning connecting roads (road 45 has curb -2 and walking -3).
Point crossPath start/end lane links at those connecting-road walking lanes.
wrong: Linking the crosswalk to the arm road's sidewalk outside the junction.

figures.caption: Figure 18. Complete advanced T junction
figures.shows: Combined OpenDRIVE view: lanes, red junction outline, connecting reference lines, three hatched crossing roads with blue reference lines, stop lines, vehicle and pedestrian lights, priority signs (UC_T_Junction.xodr).
figures.lesson: Complete signalised T: arm roads, three connecting roads, three crossing roads, stop lines, lights, controllers referenced from the junction, crossPaths.
right: List every controller of the junction's lights in <junction><controller>.
wrong: Controllers defined but not referenced by the junction (OpenSCENARIO cannot sync them).

figures.caption: Figure 19. X junction
figures.shows: X junction: N arm two-way with a curb-side BUS lane widened into a separate lane before the stop line and turn arrows; E arm two-way with lane arrows and a set-back stop line; W arm two-way with a stop line; S arm ONE-WAY inbound (blue one-way sign pointing north) with straight, right-turn and a dashed BUS+bicycle lane. Zebras on all four arms, vehicle signals incl. bus (white-bar) aspects and arrow aspects, pedestrian signals, give-way triangles, no-entry disk on the S side.
figures.lesson: X junctions differ geometrically from a T: start from scratch rather than extending a T; handle one-way arms, restricted lanes, shared stop lines.
right: Model a one-way inbound arm with lanes on one side only.
wrong: Extending a T junction model by appending a fourth arm.

figures.caption: Figure 20. Road reference lines at the X junction
figures.shows: Blue reference lines: road 7 (N) runs southward and ends at the N stop line, before the zebra; road 6 (E) runs westward and ends before the E zebra; road 4 (W) runs eastward ending before the W zebra; road 5 (S one-way) starts at the S mouth and runs southward along the WEST edge of the carriageway. Reference lines of N and E are offset from the visible centre line.
figures.lesson: Arm reference lines must stop before any cross path in the junction; their direction does not matter; a reference line need not be on the painted centre line.
right: End arm reference lines before the crosswalk so the crosswalk lies inside the junction.
Place the reference line where convenient (edge of one-way road) and use laneOffset to align lanes.
wrong: Ending the arm inside the zebra area.
Forcing the reference line onto the painted centre line.

figures.caption: Figure 21. Lane types at the X junction in ASAM OpenDRIVE view
figures.shows: Lane ids per arm. N road 7: -4 walk, -3 curb, -2,-1 driving | 0 | 1 driving, 2 curb, 3 walk. E road 6: -4,-3 walk/curb, -2,-1 driving | 0 | 1 driving, 2 curb, 3 walk. W road 4: 4,3 walk/curb, 2,1 driving | 0 | -1 driving, -2 curb, -3 walk. S road 5 (one-way, reference line pointing S): lane 0 at the W edge, left lanes 1,2,3 driving (northbound towards junction), 4 curb, 5 walk; right side -1 curb, -2 walk. Junction outline in red encloses the four zebras and corner sidewalks.
figures.lesson: A one-way inbound road with reference line pointing away gets only positive (left) driving lanes, plus curb/walking lanes on both sides; laneOffset aligns lane 0 away from the reference line on road 5.
right: One-way: put all driving lanes on the side whose travel direction matches (left lanes travel against s).
Still add curb+walking on the other side (right -1 curb, -2 walking).
wrong: Using negative lanes on a one-way road whose reference line points opposite to traffic.
Dropping the sidewalk on the lane-less side of a one-way road.

figures.caption: Figure 22. Widened lanes and additional lane in lane section
figures.shows: N arm road 7 alone: first lane section with -1,-2 (plus curb/sidewalk); the carriageway widens and a dashed black line marks a new lane section where three lanes -1,-2,-3 exist (two turn-arrowed lanes and the bus lane); a grey stop line across all three at the road end, the red junction outline and the zebra beyond.
figures.lesson: To split a lane before the junction, widen it and start a new lane section where the inner lane has two successors (-1 -> -1 and -2); this is preferred over other approaches.
right: Widen first, then start a lane section; give the splitting lane two <successor> entries.
Renumber outer lanes in the new section and link them one-to-one (old -2 -> new -3, etc.).
wrong: Inserting a zero-width lane without links, or starting a new road for the extra lane.

figures.caption: Figure 23. Restricted lanes for buses and cyclists
figures.shows: Lane-coloured X with 'BUS' markings on the N arm outer southbound lane and a 'BUS' + bicycle shared lane on the S arm's outer lane; stop lines drawn as grey bars; junction interior white (no connecting roads yet).
figures.lesson: Restricted lanes stay type driving and get <access rule=allow> with restriction bus (and bicycle for shared lanes) from the point where the restriction starts (sOffset).
right: Keep type driving and add access allow restrictions (bus, bicycle) with sOffset.
wrong: Using lane type bus/biking for a lane cyclists and buses share, or dropping the restriction at a lane-section change.

figures.caption: Figure 24. Connecting roads
figures.shows: Blue connecting reference lines: from N to W and E (and from the N arm end points), from E to W (straight) and N (right), from W to E (straight) and N, from S to N (straight) and to W and E; arrows end at the W, E and N arm ends. No connecting road ends at the S arm because it is one-way inbound.
figures.lesson: Only permitted relations get connecting roads; a one-way inbound arm is only a start of paths; several parallel connecting roads per relation are allowed for multi-lane turns.
right: Generate connecting roads only for legal turn relations (respect one-way and turn restrictions).
wrong: Creating connecting roads into a one-way inbound arm.

figures.caption: Figure 25. Pedestrian crossings
figures.shows: Same as Fig. 24 plus hatched crossing roads with blue reference lines across all four arms inside the junction, each spanning sidewalk to sidewalk; grey curb lines inside the junction follow the corner connecting roads.
figures.lesson: Each arm's zebra becomes a crossing road + crossPath in the junction.
right: One crossing road and one crossPath per zebra (split at islands when needed).
wrong: Omitting crossPaths for crosswalks on one-way arms.

figures.caption: Figure 26. Complete X junction
figures.shows: Complete X in OpenDRIVE view with signals (vehicle, arrow, bus and pedestrian lights), signs (yield, mandatory direction, one-way, no-entry) at their physical positions (UC_X_Junction.xodr).
figures.lesson: Complete X: shared stop line signal on one lane with signalReference on the others and on connecting roads (Code 27).
right: Define a stop line once (validity on one lane) and reuse it with <signalReference> for other lanes/roads.
wrong: Duplicating the same physical stop line as several signals.

figures.caption: Figure 27. Complete junction
figures.shows: Same image as Figure 1: signalised 5-road junction with one-way roads (SW inbound, SE outbound), pedestrian crossings, bus lanes and a splitter island on the N arm.
figures.lesson: The full case: start from scratch rather than extending the X junction.
right: Build multi-arm junctions as one common junction with all arms.
wrong: Chaining an X junction and a T junction to represent a 5-arm node.

figures.caption: Figure 28. 5-road junction with two one-way roads
figures.shows: 5-arm geometry without signals: N arm with splitter teardrop island and crossings split in two halves; E, W arms two-way; SW arm one-way inbound (bus/bike lane); SE arm one-way OUTBOUND (blue sign arrow pointing away, no-entry disk at its mouth, yield triangles on W and N).
figures.lesson: An outgoing one-way road is not an incoming road: it never appears as incomingRoad in <connection>, only as successor of connecting roads.
right: Do not list outgoing-only arms as incomingRoad.
wrong: Creating connections with incomingRoad = an exit-only one-way road.

figures.caption: Figure 29. Connecting roads
figures.shows: Blue connecting reference lines including curves into the SE arm: its reference line starts at the junction outline and points SE; connecting roads from N, E, W and SW arms terminate at that start point. The SE arm has only blue (right/negative) lanes. Grey curb lines inside the junction show the corner connecting roads; the N-arm splitter outline is visible.
figures.lesson: Outgoing one-way road appears only as successor of connecting roads.
right: Terminate connecting roads at the outgoing road's start with contactPoint start.
wrong: Making the outgoing arm a predecessor of any connecting road.

figures.caption: Figure 30. Junction reference line
figures.shows: Red straight arrow drawn across the N part of the junction (WSW->ENE), passing near the N arm end: this is the junction's own planView line used as a local frame for objects (the traffic island) that belong to the junction.
figures.lesson: A junction may get its own <planView> reference line (1.8) to position junction objects (e.g. trafficIsland via cornerLocal) independent of any road.
right: Use a junction reference line when objects span several connecting roads.
wrong: Attaching a junction-wide island to a single arbitrary connecting road.

figures.caption: Figure 31. Complete 5-road junction
figures.shows: Complete 5-road junction in OpenDRIVE view: all connecting roads, crossings on all five arms (incl. SE), signals and signs (UC_5Road_Junction.xodr).
figures.lesson: Complete multi-arm junction incl. boundary, elevation grid, restricted island lane, junction objects.
right: Close the junction with <boundary> (lane and joint segments) and an <elevationGrid> matching arm elevations.
wrong: Leaving junction surface height undefined between connecting roads.

figures.caption: Figure 32. Bidirectional junction
figures.shows: Incoming road 1 (W, two lanes 1 and -1) and incoming roads 2 (E) and 3 (S) each with a single lane -1 usable in both directions (@direction=both). Orange connecting roads: road 5 and road 6 between roads 1 and 2 (one per direction, each single lane -1), road 4 (@direction=both, lane -1) curving between road 3 and road 2.
figures.lesson: A single bidirectional lane connects via one connecting road with direction both, referenced by two connections (one from each end).
right: Use one connecting road with direction both and two <connection>s (contactPoint start from one side, end from the other).
Use separate one-way connecting roads where the other road has separate lanes per direction.
wrong: Creating two overlapping connecting roads for a single-lane bidirectional link.

figures.chapter: 7 Junctions with entry and exit lanes
figures.caption: Figure 33. Motorway with entry lanes and exit lanes
figures.shows: Dual carriageway motorway with green median. Upper carriageway (traffic leftward): an exit lane branches up-left; a solid line separates the diverging lane from the adjacent lane over the overlap stretch before the physical split. Lower carriageway (traffic rightward): an entry ramp comes from the lower left and runs parallel as an acceleration lane, with a dashed line from the gore point onward.
figures.lesson: Two entry/exit types: non-overlapping (the lanes never share area) and overlapping (the exit lane shares area with a main lane until it separates).
right: Classify each ramp junction as overlapping or non-overlapping before choosing where to cut.
wrong: Treating every ramp as a common junction.

figures.chapter: 7 Junctions with entry and exit lanes
figures.caption: Figure 34. Motorway with an entry
figures.shows: One carriageway (median on top, traffic left->right) with two lanes; a ramp approaches from the lower left and joins as a third lane exactly where the lane-divider dashes start (gore point).
figures.lesson: Non-overlapping entry: the ramp lane continues as an extra outer lane with no shared area.
right: Recognise a parallel acceleration lane starting at the gore.
wrong: Merging the ramp lane directly into an existing main lane.

figures.chapter: 7 Junctions with entry and exit lanes
figures.caption: Figure 35. Direct junction
figures.shows: Same scene with a yellow circle around the gore point where the ramp edge meets the main carriageway edge.
figures.lesson: Place the direct junction where the entry joins the main road (at the gore).
right: Cut all involved roads at the gore point of a merge.
wrong: Cutting far upstream or downstream of the gore.

figures.chapter: 7 Junctions with entry and exit lanes
figures.caption: Figure 36. Road reference lines
figures.shows: Vertical red line = direct junction cut at the gore. Main road reference line runs along the median edge and stops at the cut; the downstream road starts at the cut on the same line. The ramp reference line runs along its left edge and ends at the cut at the boundary between main lane -2 and the new outer lane of the downstream road.
figures.lesson: All three roads start/end at the direct-junction cut; the ramp ends at a lateral offset from the downstream reference line (direct junctions link lanes directly, no connecting road).
right: End/start all roads at one cut line; link lanes in the direct junction.
wrong: Building connecting roads for a simple merge.

figures.chapter: 7 Junctions with entry and exit lanes
figures.caption: Figure 37. Motorway with a non-overlapping entry
figures.shows: Road 315 (lanes -1,-2 driving, light blue) and ramp road 292 (lane -1 onRamp, yellow) end at the red cut; road 313 starts there with -1,-2 driving and -3 entry (pale yellow).
figures.lesson: Lane types: onRamp before the junction on the ramp road, entry for the outermost lane after it, driving for the rest; no overlap, no crossing -> direct junction.
right: Ramp lane type onRamp; acceleration lane on the main road type entry.
wrong: Typing the acceleration lane as driving or the ramp as entry.

figures.chapter: 7 Junctions with entry and exit lanes
figures.caption: Figure 38. Motorway with an exit
figures.shows: Carriageway (median at bottom, traffic right->left) with three lanes on the right part; the outer lane curves away up-left; a solid line separates the exit from the next lane over a stretch where both still share the paved area; the exit becomes a 2-lane ramp.
figures.lesson: Overlapping exit: exit lane and adjacent main lane share area over the overlap stretch.
right: Identify the overlap stretch between the cut and the physical separation.
wrong: Ignoring the overlap and placing the cut at the physical gore only.

figures.chapter: 7 Junctions with entry and exit lanes
figures.caption: Figure 39. Direct junction
figures.shows: Yellow circle placed where the exit lane starts to branch (where the full-width exit lane begins to curve away), upstream of the physical separation.
figures.lesson: Place the direct junction where the exit branches from the main road; direct junctions allow one overlapping lane.
right: Cut at the start of the branching, not at the physical gore.
wrong: Using a common junction when only one lane overlaps and no traffic crosses.

figures.chapter: 7 Junctions with entry and exit lanes
figures.caption: Figure 40. Road reference lines
figures.shows: Red vertical cut; main road reference line along the median edge (bottom) ending at the cut and the downstream main road starting there; the exit road reference line starts at the cut at the boundary between main lanes -1 and -2 and curves up-left, so its first lane lies over main lane -2.
figures.lesson: The exit road starts at the cut inside the main carriageway, so its lane overlaps the downstream main lane until it separates.
right: Start the exit road's reference line at the cut at the lateral position of its innermost lane.
wrong: Starting the exit road only where it is physically separated.

figures.chapter: 7 Junctions with entry and exit lanes
figures.caption: Figure 41. Motorway with an overlapping exit
figures.shows: Road 300 (-1,-2 driving, -3 exit) ends at the cut; road 305 (-1,-2 driving) continues; road 308 starts with lane -1 exit (overlapping 305's lane -2, labelled overlapZone) and lane -2 offRamp; a dotted line marks road 308's second lane section where lane -1 becomes offRamp after the overlap.
figures.lesson: Before cut: outermost lane exit; after cut: overlapping lane exit, outer exiting lane offRamp; new lane section on the exit road after the overlap switches exit->offRamp; set @overlapZone on the lane links of the overlapping lanes.
right: Use lane sections on the exit road: overlapping part (type exit) then offRamp.
Set overlapZone at least as long as the overlap but as small as possible.
wrong: Leaving lane type exit for the whole ramp.
Omitting overlapZone so tools think lanes collide.

figures.caption: Figure 42. Slip lanes
figures.shows: Signalised 4-arm crossing of two dual carriageways (green medians, N at top, RHT). In each corner a free right-turn slip lane bypasses the central junction: NW (southbound -> westbound), NE (westbound -> northbound), SE (northbound -> eastbound), SW (eastbound -> southbound). Some slip lanes start from a parallel deceleration lane and/or end in a parallel acceleration lane, others branch/merge directly with a taper. Signals and stop lines are only at the central intersection.
figures.lesson: Slip lanes start/end at the outermost lane, are one-way, cross no other traffic of the same junction, yield where they merge, usually have no lights.
right: Detect free right turns (left in LHT) that bypass the main node and model them separately.
wrong: Routing slip-lane traffic through the central common junction.

figures.caption: Figure 43. Large junction with variations of slip lanes
figures.shows: Same junction without labels; variations: slip lane branching after a parallel exit lane, slip lane merging into a parallel entry lane, slip lanes branching/merging with tapers only.
figures.lesson: Large junction with several slip-lane variants to choose junction types for.
right: Choose junction type per split/merge point.
wrong: One giant common junction covering all slip lanes.

figures.caption: Figure 44. Direct junctions
figures.shows: Eight yellow circles: at every point where a slip lane splits from or merges into a straight carriageway (two on each arm: one on the inbound carriageway diverge, one on the outbound carriageway merge).
figures.lesson: Use a direct junction at every split/merge of slip lane and straight road; lanes may overlap if direction is the same and no traffic crosses.
right: Direct junction at each slip-lane diverge and merge.
wrong: Common junction for a simple same-direction split/merge.

figures.caption: Figure 45. Simplified direct junctions
figures.shows: N arm: the two circles replaced by one ellipse spanning both carriageways (diverge and merge at the same station). W arm: one tall ellipse spanning both carriageways. E and S arms keep two separate circles because their diverge and merge are at different stations.
figures.lesson: Direct junctions at the same position for both directions can be combined into one, if model accuracy allows.
right: Combine opposite-direction split/merge points at the same station into one direct junction.
wrong: Combining points at clearly different stations.

figures.caption: Figure 46. Common junction
figures.shows: One yellow circle around the central intersection area (between the four stop lines).
figures.lesson: The centre, where straight traffic and crossing turns meet, is a common junction.
right: Common junction only for the crossing area.
wrong: Using direct junctions where traffic crosses.

figures.caption: Figure 47. Straight road reference lines
figures.shows: Red lines = direct junction cuts (N: one cut across both carriageways; W: one cut across both; E: separate cuts on each carriageway; S: separate cuts); red rectangle = central common junction. Blue reference lines run on the medians: S->N (from bottom edge to S cut, S cut to centre, centre to N cut, N cut to top) and E->W (right edge to E cut, E cut to centre, centre to W cut, W cut to left edge).
figures.lesson: Junctions define where roads are needed; between a combined direct junction and the centre one road (both carriageways, reference line on the median) suffices.
right: Place one reference line on the median for both carriageways between combined junctions.
wrong: Separate roads per carriageway where one road would do.

figures.caption: Figure 48. Straight road reference lines for opposite direction of travel
figures.shows: Additional blue reference lines for the carriageways whose direct junctions are not combined: southbound centre->S (beside the median, with a further road beyond the S cut) and eastbound centre->E (beside the median, beyond the E cut).
figures.lesson: Where the two directions are cut at different stations, each direction needs its own road.
right: Split into per-direction roads only where cut positions differ.
wrong: Forcing a single two-way road across non-aligned cuts.

figures.caption: Figure 49. Road reference lines for slip lanes
figures.shows: Four curved blue reference lines, one per slip lane, each running from one direct-junction cut to another (e.g. NW: from N cut inside the southbound carriageway to the W cut at the north edge).
figures.lesson: Each slip lane is its own road between two direct junctions.
right: Slip-lane road from diverge cut to merge cut.
wrong: Slip lanes as connecting roads of the central junction.

figures.caption: Figure 50. Road reference lines inside the central junction
figures.shows: Central red rectangle with connecting reference lines: straight N->S, S->N, E->W, W->E and curved left turns; no right turns inside the centre because those use slip lanes.
figures.lesson: Central junction follows chapter 6 rules; right-turn relations served by slip lanes are omitted from it.
right: Do not duplicate slip-lane relations inside the central junction.
wrong: Adding right-turn connecting roads in the centre as well.

figures.caption: Figure 51. Lanes with @type="entry" or @type="exit"
figures.shows: Coloured lanes: entry (yellow) on the W arm north edge after the NW merge and on the E arm south edge after the SE merge; exit (blue) on the W arm south edge before the SW diverge and on the S arm east edge before the SE diverge.
figures.lesson: Parallel acceleration/deceleration sections belong to the main road and are typed entry/exit.
right: Parallel deceleration lane = exit on the main road; acceleration lane = entry.
wrong: Typing the parallel lanes slipLane or giving them their own road.

figures.caption: Figure 52. Lanes with @type="slipLane"
figures.shows: Four green curved slip-lane roads labelled slipLane between their direct-junction cuts.
figures.lesson: The slip lane itself is type slipLane (1.8).
right: Type the slip-lane road's lane slipLane.
wrong: Typing it driving or connectingRamp in a 1.8 output.

figures.caption: Figure 53. Lanes with @type="driving"
figures.shows: All remaining lanes coloured: light blue (right-side lanes) and beige (left-side lanes: N arm southbound and W arm eastbound carriageways, travelling against the median reference line), grey central junction.
figures.lesson: All other lanes are driving; one road per arm carries both carriageways with the reference line on the median.
right: Default lane type driving.
wrong: Leaving lane types none.

figures.caption: Figure 54. Slip lanes overlapping other lanes
figures.shows: White brackets labelled overlapZone at the NW slip start (overlapping the southbound outer lane below the N cut), the NE slip end near the N cut and the NE slip start near the E cut, and the SW slip end above the S cut; overlap brackets are slightly longer than the shaded overlap.
figures.lesson: Set overlapZone on the laneLink to cover the whole overlap, chosen slightly larger than needed.
right: overlapZone >= overlap length (slightly larger).
wrong: overlapZone shorter than the overlap.

figures.caption: Figure 55. Roads with traffic lights and stop line
figures.shows: Perspective: road 4 (lanes 1 beige, -1 blue, s/t axes drawn) ends, road 46 continues; stop line signal 1 across lane -1 at the end of road 4; signal 2 on a mast arm above the lane and signal 4 on the pole at the roadside, both on road 46.
figures.lesson: One stop line serves two lights located on another road.
right: Lights at physical position (road 46), stop line on road 4.
wrong: Moving lights to road 4.

figures.caption: Figure 56. References and dependencies between traffic lights and stop line
figures.shows: Same scene with arrows: yellow 'reference id=1' arrows from each light down to stop line 1; orange 'dependency id=2' and 'dependency id=4' arrows from the stop line up to the lights. (The page text below the figure states the directions the other way round; the drawing matches the rules in 9.2 and Codes 38-39.)
figures.lesson: Light -> stop line via <reference elementType=signal type=stopLine>; stop line -> each light via <dependency type=trafficLight>.
right: Bidirectional wiring: reference on lights, dependency on stop line.
wrong: Only one direction of linkage.
Following the swapped description in the text under Figure 56.

figures.caption: Figure 57. T-junction with three traffic lights and two stop lines
figures.shows: T junction: road 1 (S, reference line pointing S from the junction, lanes 1 left-turn and 2 straight approach northward) with two staggered stop lines 203 (lane 1, s=3) and 204 (lane 2, s=4); road 2 (N, reference line pointing N) with signal 102 on a mast at its E side beyond the junction; road 3 (W, reference line pointing W, lanes 1-3 eastbound) with signal 105 (yellow/green left arrows) at the NW corner; signal 103 on a pole beside road 1 near the junction.
figures.lesson: Lights may be behind the junction (far-side); stop line 203 depends on 102, 103, 105; stop line 204 on 102, 103; each light references the stop lines it governs.
right: Model per-lane stop lines with validity on one lane each.
Use orientation '-' for signals on lanes travelling against s.
wrong: Giving far-side lights a validity on their own road's lanes.

figures.caption: Figure 58. A rail road crossing
figures.shows: Two-lane road crossing a single railway track at an angle; St. Andrew's crosses at the right of each approach; each approach has a solid centre line ending in a transverse stop bar before the track.
figures.lesson: Crossings: traffic of two roads crosses but cannot change roads.
right: Use a crossing junction for rail level crossings.
wrong: Common junction with connecting roads for a rail crossing.

figures.caption: Figure 59. Pedestrian crossing
figures.shows: Straight road with sidewalks top and bottom, two lanes in one direction (upper) and one (lower); a hatched painted island with two green raised halves and a paved gap in the middle (pedestrian refuge) between the directions.
figures.lesson: Mid-block pedestrian crossing through a refuge island.
right: Model mid-block crossings with a virtual junction and crossPath.
wrong: Cutting the main road into pieces for a mid-block crossing.

figures.caption: Figure 60. Road reference line
figures.shows: Blue reference line of the general-traffic road running left->right along the lower edge of the island (lane divider between the single lane and the island).
figures.lesson: The main road stays one continuous road through the crossing.
right: Keep the main road continuous.
wrong: Splitting the road at the crossing.

figures.caption: Figure 61. Lanes on the road for general traffic
figures.shows: Road 1: left 1,2 driving (beige), 3 curb (violet strip), 4 walking (dark red); right -1 driving (blue), -2 curb, -3 walking.
figures.lesson: Main road cross-section incl. curbs and sidewalks.
right: driving + curb + walking per side.
wrong: Omitting sidewalks that the crossing must connect.

figures.caption: Figure 62. Restricted lane and changed lane width
figures.shows: Dotted lines mark lane-section boundaries; in the middle section a new lane 1 of type restricted (orange) opens next to the reference line, widens to full width, holds, and narrows again; left lanes shift to ids 2,3 driving, 4 curb, 5 walking; outside the section ids revert to 1,2,3,4.
figures.lesson: The traffic island is a restricted lane inserted with its own lane section and cubic widths; outer lanes renumber and are linked across sections.
right: Insert island as restricted lane in a dedicated lane section; link renumbered lanes.
wrong: Using an object only and leaving the drivable area overlapping the island.

figures.caption: Figure 63. Road reference line of the pedestrian crossing
figures.shows: Road 2 reference line perpendicular to road 1, from the middle of the bottom walking lane -3 to the middle of the top walking lane 5, crossing the island at its widest part.
figures.lesson: Crossing road starts and ends in the middle of the walking lanes it connects.
right: Start/end crossing reference line at sidewalk centres.
wrong: Ending the crossing at the curb line.

figures.caption: Figure 64. All lanes of the pedestrian crossing
figures.shows: Road 2 with a single walking lane -1 (dark red) on the right of its reference line, spanning road 1 from sidewalk to sidewalk over the island.
figures.lesson: Crossing road has one walking lane.
right: One walking lane on the crossing road.
wrong: Driving lanes on a crossing road.

figures.caption: Figure 65. Virtual junction for the pedestrian crossing
figures.shows: Red dashed lines on road 1 marking @sStart and @sEnd of the virtual junction, tightly around the crossing walking lane.
figures.lesson: Virtual junction with mainRoad=1 and sStart/sEnd clearly outside the area of crossing traffic.
right: sStart/sEnd bracket the crossing with margin.
wrong: sStart/sEnd inside the crossing width.

figures.caption: Figure 66. Complete pedestrian crossing
figures.shows: Complete view: island hatching and lane markings added, crossing road over the refuge.
figures.lesson: Complete mid-block crossing: main road uncut, crossing road junction=virtual id, crossPath with start/end lane links, priority high=main low=crossing.
right: Main road junction=-1; crossing road junction=virtual junction id.
wrong: Setting the main road's junction attribute to the virtual junction.

figures.caption: Figure 67. A rail road crossing
figures.shows: Same image as Figure 58: rail track with priority crossing a two-lane road.
figures.lesson: Rail crossing: crossing junction, rail has priority.
right: priority high = rail road.
wrong: Road priority over rail.

figures.caption: Figure 68. Road reference lines
figures.shows: Road 1 (vehicle road) reference line S->N along its centre; road 2 (rail) reference line WSW->ENE along the track centre; both pass straight through the crossing point without cuts.
figures.lesson: Both roads stay continuous; neither is part of the junction.
right: Do not cut road or rail at a level crossing.
wrong: Splitting both roads at the crossing point.

figures.caption: Figure 69. Lanes on the roads
figures.shows: Road 1 lanes 1 (beige) and -1 (blue) driving; road 2 single lane -1 of type rail (dark blue).
figures.lesson: Rail road gets a rail lane.
right: Rail lane type rail.
wrong: Track modelled as a driving lane.

figures.caption: Figure 70. Road sections
figures.shows: @sStart/@sEnd tick marks on both roads bracketing the crossing area: on road 1 below and above the track, on road 2 left and right of the road.
figures.lesson: Crossing junction holds one roadSection per road with sStart/sEnd outside the crossing area.
right: roadSection per road; margins outside the overlap.
wrong: roadSection limits inside the overlap.

figures.caption: Figure 71. Complete rail road crossing
figures.shows: Complete: St. Andrew's crosses at each approach, centre lines with stop bars before the track as grey markings.
figures.lesson: Add road markings and signs to the crossing.
right: Signs + stop markings on the road before the track.
wrong: No warning signs.

guideline.source: ASAM OpenDRIVE Junction Guideline 1.0.0 (2023-11-22), non-normative, written for ASAM OpenDRIVE 1.8.0. Read in full from the local mirror docs/reference/asam_opendrive_junction_guideline_1.0.0 (16 HTML pages); all 69 figure images (71 figure numbers; Fig. 1/27 and 58/67 reuse one image) were opened and inspected - see figures_guideline.json. Example files named by the guideline (UC_T_Junction.xodr, UC_X_Junction.xodr, UC_5Road_Junction.xodr, Ex_Bidirectional_Junction.xodr, Ex_Entry_Exit.xodr, Ex_Slip_Lane.xodr, Ex_Pedestrian_Crossing.xodr) are not in the mirror.
opendrive_1_7_compatibility: The guideline targets 1.8.0. 1.8-only features it relies on: lane types walking and slipLane; @overlapZone on direct-junction laneLink; junction type crossing with <roadSection>; <crossPath> with start/endLaneLink; junction <planView>, <boundary> (lane/joint segments, transitionLength), <elevationGrid>, junction <objects>; signal <semantics> (priority yield/stopLine/trafficLight/waitingLine); lane @direction=both on connecting roads.

Available already in 1.7: common/direct/virtual junctions, lane types curb, sidewalk, restricted, entry, exit, onRamp, offRamp, connectingRamp, bidirectional, rail, tram, bus, biking; lane <height> inner/outer; lane <access> restrictions; signal <validity>, <dependency>, <reference>, <signalReference>; <controller> and junction <controller>; junction <priority>; object outlines with cornerLocal, borders, type trafficIsland.

Down-mapping for a 1.7 / CARLA target: walking -> sidewalk; slipLane -> driving (or connectingRamp); overlapping direct junction -> move the cut to the first non-overlapping station or use a common junction; drop overlapZone; crossing junction -> leave both roads uncut and express priority with signals/signs; crossPath -> crosswalk object on the road plus optional walking road without junction linkage; drop junction boundary/elevationGrid (keep connecting-road elevation consistent instead); drop signal semantics but keep type/subtype.
The guideline itself mixes 'sidewalk' (X junction, Code 25-26) and 'walking' (T junction) for the same thing; for 1.8 output use walking.

chapters.title: Preface, scope, terms, abbreviations, backward compatibility
chapters.summary: Foreword places the guideline as a non-normative companion to the 1.8 spec next to the (normative) Signal reference 1.0.0. The introduction gives the use-case table that maps real situations to junction types and states that examples grow in complexity. Scope: best practice for modelling real junctions so producers and consumers share expectations. Terms: gore point = point of no return where a lane splits (theoretical gore = separating markings, physical gore = curb/grass triangle); overlapping = at least one lane of each road covers the same area; non-overlapping = no shared lane area (bridges/tunnels are not overlapping). First release, no backward-compatibility notes.
guidance: Pick the junction type from the use-case table before building geometry: common for T/X/multi-arm/roundabouts, direct for same-level splits/merges (ramps, slip lanes), virtual for driveways, parking accesses and mid-block crossings, crossing for rail level crossings.
Where the use-case table says 'common (non-constant elevation)', fall back to a common junction only when the direct/virtual junction would need varying elevation across it.
Locate gore points (theoretical gore where the separating marking starts, physical gore where curb/grass begins) - they are the cut positions for arm roads and direct junctions.
Classify each split/merge as overlapping or non-overlapping using lane areas, ignoring grade-separated structures (bridges/tunnels never count as overlapping).
Look up traffic-light/stop-line type codes in the Signal reference 1.0.0 (country=OpenDRIVE) rather than inventing them.
right: Common junction for intersections where traffic crosses or changes roads with crossing paths.
Direct junction where roads only split/merge at the same level.
Treat bridges and tunnels as separate, non-overlapping roads.
wrong: Using a common junction for every OSM node with degree > 2.
Treating a bridge over a road as an overlapping junction.

use_cases.how: Table says common. The guideline gives no geometry; one reasonable reading is a common junction per entry/exit node of the ring (ring segments as ordinary roads) for large roundabouts, or a single common junction for a compact one - this is an inference, not guideline text.
Virtual junction on the main road (mainRoad, sStart, sEnd) with the access road connected without cutting the main road; common only if elevation varies.

chapters.title: Backward compatibility
guidance: None.

chapters.title: Common junctions
chapters.summary: Common junctions are where drivers change roads and cross other traffic (T/Y, X, more arms). Rules: arm reference lines start/end at the junction outline; junction area as small as possible but as big as necessary; connecting roads continuous with the incoming roads; only connecting roads of the same junction may overlap each other. Worked examples: basic T (lanes, junction, connecting roads, connections, lane links incl. curb/sidewalk, priority signs, markings), lowered curb/sidewalk at crossings (lane heights), advanced T (stop lines, lights, references/dependencies, controllers, crossing roads with invisible stop lines and pedestrian lights, crossPath), X junction (reference lines before cross paths, one-way arm, laneOffset, lane widening with two successors, bus/bike access, shared stop line via signalReference), 5-road junction (outgoing one-way road, restricted island lane, gap-free laneOffset, outward-shifted reference line for wide connecting roads, junction reference line, traffic island object, boundary, elevation grid, transition length) and bidirectional single-lane arms (connecting road with direction both used by two connections).
guidance: Rules (6.2): every arm road's reference line starts or ends exactly at the junction outline; nothing of an arm lies inside the junction.
Size the junction area as small as possible but large enough to contain all crossing/turning movements and the crosswalks (smaller = cheaper to compute).
Connecting roads must be continuous (position and heading, i.e. G1) with the arm roads at both ends (spec 10.3 road linkage).
Only connecting roads may overlap other connecting roads of the same junction - arm roads must not overlap the junction or each other.
T step 1: place arm reference lines so they end/start at the gore points (curb-return tangent points) outside the junction; direction is free; arm roads get junction=-1.
T step 2: give each arm its full cross-section per side: driving lane(s), a curb lane at the outside, a walking lane next to the curb (ids outward from 0).
T step 3: create the junction and set it as successor (arm ends at junction) or predecessor (arm starts at junction) in each arm's <link>.

T step 4: create one connecting road per arm pair/path with junction=<id>; its predecessor/successor are the arm roads with contactPoint start/end according to which end of the arm touches the junction.

T step 5: add one <connection> per (incoming road, connecting road) pair - with two-way arms every arm is an incoming road, so a two-way connecting road appears in two connections (contactPoint start from one arm, end from the other).

T step 6: give connecting roads driving lanes for each direction; on the side that follows the junction outline add curb and walking lanes so curbs and sidewalks continue through the junction (road 46 left side lanes 2 curb, 3 walking; road 45 right side -2 curb, -3 walking round the corner).

T step 7: add <laneLink from=incoming lane to=connecting lane> for every permitted relation - driving lanes AND the curb/walking lanes carried by that connecting road (Code 7 links -1,-2,-3 of road 4 to -1,-2,-3 of road 45).

T step 8: put lane predecessor/successor links only on connecting-road lanes (each connecting road touches exactly one arm at each end); leave arm-road lanes without links into the junction (an arm end may feed several connecting roads).

T step 9: set priority with sign signals on the incoming roads near the junction (s at the road end, t on the traffic side, orientation for the approaching direction, validity on the inbound lane(s)); add <semantics><priority type="yield"/> on yield/stop signs; supplementary plates (bent priority) are separate signals at the same position.
T step 10: add road marks: broken centre line on arms (laneChange both), edge lines continued along the outline connecting roads, a guide line for a bent priority route on its connecting road.

Lowered curb at a crossing: on the curb lane use <height> inner=outer=0.12 at the approach, ramp to 0.02 over 0.5 m, hold over the crossing width, ramp back to 0.12; on the walking lane lower only the inner (curb-side) edge to 0.02 and keep outer at 0.12.
Advanced T: add a stop line signal on each incoming road at its junction end with validity on the inbound lanes and <semantics><priority type="stopLine"/>.

Place traffic lights as signals at their physical location (country=OpenDRIVE, type per Signal reference, dynamic=yes, semantics trafficLight) - this is usually the start of a connecting road (s~2.5) or a far-side road, not the stop-line road.
Give each light <reference id=stopline elementType=signal type=stopLine/>; give each stop line <dependency id=light type=trafficLight/> for every light that governs it.
Define <controller> with one <control signalId> per light of a phase group and list each controller in the junction (<junction><controller id type/>) so OpenSCENARIO can sync them.

Model each pedestrian crossing inside the junction as an extra road with junction=<id>, one walking lane (width ~3 m) and crosswalk-style broken road marks; its reference line spans sidewalk to sidewalk just beyond the stop line.

Put invisible stop lines (country=OpenDRIVE type=11000001, semantics waitingLine) on the crossing road near both kerbs, each depending on the pedestrian light that faces it; pedestrian lights (type 1000002) reference the invisible stop line at the opposite kerb.
Add a controller for the pedestrian lights and list it in the junction.

Add <crossPath id crossingRoad=<crossing road> roadAtStart=<connecting road at start> roadAtEnd=<connecting road at end>> with <startLaneLink s from=<walking lane of roadAtStart> to=<crossing lane>> and <endLaneLink ...>; s is measured on roadAtStart/roadAtEnd.
X junction: model from scratch (do not extend a T). End arm reference lines before any crosswalk/cross path; direction is irrelevant; reference line need not be the painted centre line.

One-way inbound arm whose reference line points away: put the driving lanes on the left (positive ids); still add curb/walking on the other side; use <laneOffset> to align lane 0 when it is not on the reference line.

Turn-lane split before the stop line: widen the lane with width polynomials, start a new lane section where the extra lane exists, give the splitting lane two <successor> ids; this beats other approaches.
Bus/bike lanes: keep type driving and add <access rule="allow" sOffset><restriction type="bus"/></access> (add bicycle for shared lanes); repeat it in the next lane section with the new lane id.
Create connecting roads only for permitted driving relations (respect one-way arms and turn restrictions); add crossing roads + crossPaths for each crosswalk.
A stop line spanning several lanes is one signal (validity on one lane, width = full width) plus <signalReference> with validity for further lanes or on connecting roads.
5-road junction: model from scratch. An outgoing one-way road is not an incoming road - it never appears as incomingRoad; it is only successor of connecting roads.
Traffic island in an arm: add a lane of type restricted that widens linearly from 0 (width b>0) to make room for the island.
Avoid gaps: connecting-road laneOffset a = width of the lanes it skips and b = matching slope so lane edges and heading coincide with the preceding road.
Wide connecting roads on tight corners: shift the reference line outward (equal laneOffset a and lane width a) so the inner sidewalk edge never gets a negative radius.

Optionally give the junction its own <planView> reference line and place junction-wide objects (trafficIsland with cornerLocal outline, concrete fill, curb border useCompleteOutline) in junction <objects>.

Define the junction <boundary> as an ordered loop of segments: type lane (roadId, borderLane, sStart/sEnd on connecting roads along the outline) alternating with type joint (roadId of the arm, contactPoint, jointLaneStart..jointLaneEnd across the arm mouth); add transitionLength on joints.
Add a junction <elevationGrid> (gridSpacing, gridVectors left/center/right) that matches the elevations of all incoming/outgoing roads at their joints.

Bidirectional single-lane arms: create one connecting road whose lane has direction both and reference it from two connections (incoming road A contactPoint end, incoming road B contactPoint start); create normal connections for other roads.

chapters.title: Junctions with entry and exit lanes
chapters.summary: Entries/exits on motorways and rural roads let drivers join/leave on dedicated acceleration/deceleration lanes. Recommendation: direct junction (one cut instead of two, one overlapping lane allowed); use a common junction if traffic of different lanes crosses or more than one lane overlaps. Overlap zone as small as possible. Non-overlapping entry: cut at the gore point, ramp lane onRamp before the cut, outermost lane entry after it. Overlapping exit: cut where the exit branches; before the cut outermost lane exit; the exit road starts inside the carriageway with an exit lane overlapping the main lane, then a new lane section turns it into offRamp; outer ramp lane offRamp; overlapZone on the lane links.
guidance: Decide overlapping vs non-overlapping for each ramp: does any lane of the ramp share area with a main-road lane after the split/before the merge?
If traffic crosses or more than one lane overlaps -> common junction; otherwise -> direct junction (preferred: one cut).
Non-overlapping entry: put the direct junction at the gore point where the ramp edge meets the carriageway edge; end the main road and the ramp road at that cut and start the downstream road there.
Lane types (entry): ramp lane before the cut = onRamp; outermost lane after the cut = entry (acceleration lane); others driving.
Overlapping exit: put the direct junction where the exit starts to branch (upstream of the physical gore); end the upstream road there; start the continuing main road and the exit road there.
Start the exit road's reference line at the cut at the lateral position of its innermost lane (inside the carriageway), so its first lane overlaps the downstream main lane until separation.

Lane types (exit): upstream outermost lane = exit; on the exit road the overlapping lane = exit in a first lane section that ends at the end of the overlap, then offRamp in a second lane section; the outer exit-road lane = offRamp; others driving.
Set @overlapZone on the laneLinks of the two overlapping lanes: at least the overlap length, as small as possible.
Apply spec road-linkage rules and lane-type rules (spec 10.3, 11.7).
right: Direct junction at the gore for merges, at the branch start for overlapping diverges.
onRamp/offRamp for ramp lanes, entry/exit for the parallel lanes on the main road.
Lane section switch exit->offRamp after the overlap.
wrong: Common junction (two cuts) for a simple ramp without crossings.
More than one overlapping lane in a direct junction.
Oversized overlapZone or none at all.

chapters.title: Slip lanes
chapters.summary: Slip lanes bypass the main intersection: start/end at the outermost lane, one-way, no crossing with other traffic of the same junction, give way where they merge, rarely signalised. Recommendation: direct junctions at every split/merge (lanes may overlap if same direction and no crossing), a common junction only for the central crossing area. Slip lanes use lane type slipLane; parallel acceleration/deceleration parts belong to the main road as entry/exit. Direct junctions at the same station for both directions may be merged into one; roads are then defined by the connections between junctions; overlapZone covers each overlap and is chosen slightly larger than needed.
guidance: Locate every point where a slip lane diverges from or merges into a straight road; put a direct junction there.
Use one common junction for the central area where straight traffic and crossing turns meet (follow chapter 6 rules inside it).
If the diverge on one carriageway and the merge on the opposite carriageway are at the same station, merge them into a single direct junction across the whole road (only if accuracy allows).

Derive roads from junction-to-junction links: between a combined direct junction and the centre, one road for both carriageways (reference line on the median); where cuts differ by direction, separate roads per direction.
Each slip lane is its own road from diverge cut to merge cut, lane type slipLane.
Parallel deceleration lanes before a slip lane are type exit on the main road; parallel acceleration lanes after it are type entry on the main road.
Do not create right-turn (RHT) connecting roads inside the central junction for relations served by slip lanes.
All other lanes driving.
Set overlapZone on the slip-lane lane links to cover the whole overlap area, slightly larger than needed.
right: Direct junction per split/merge, common junction only at the centre.
slipLane type on the bypass road; entry/exit on parallel lanes of the main road.
Combined direct junctions at equal stations.
wrong: One big common junction including slip lanes.
Slip-lane relations duplicated as connecting roads in the centre.
Typing parallel decel/accel lanes as slipLane.

chapters.title: Traffic lights
chapters.summary: Rules for lights and stop lines: lights are placed at their physical position (s/t of the road they stand at, not necessarily the road where vehicles stop); the stop line tells where to stop and is only relevant when the light is red/off, so the stop line gets a <dependency type=trafficLight> per governing light; the light gets <reference elementType=signal type=stopLine> to the stop line(s); several lights may share one stop line; lights get no lane validity - the stop line's validity applies; lights with the same phases share a controller. Examples: one stop line + two lights on another road; T junction with two per-lane stop lines governed by three lights incl. far-side lights.
guidance: Create one stop-line signal per stop position (per lane group with identical phase), on the approach road, validity fromLane/toLane = governed lanes, orientation matching travel direction (- for lanes travelling against s).

Create each light at its physical s/t on the road it stands at (connecting road, far-side road, approach road), dynamic=yes, country=OpenDRIVE with type/subtype from the Signal reference, no <validity>.
Add on every light a <reference id=<stopLine> elementType="signal" type="stopLine"/> for each stop line it governs (a light may reference several).
Add on every stop line a <dependency id=<light> type="trafficLight"/> for each light that governs it (may be several).
Signs interacting with lights may get dependencies too (optional).
Group lights with identical phases in one <controller> (e.g. all green-arrow heads of a movement) and list controllers in the junction.
Country traffic rules are outside OpenDRIVE but drive which lights govern which stop line.
right: Far-side lights referencing near-side stop lines.
Per-lane stop lines with distinct dependencies (left-turn line depends on three lights, straight line on two).
Lane validity only on stop lines.
wrong: Lane validity on the light itself.
Moving lights to the stop-line road.

chapters.title: Crossings and cross paths
chapters.summary: Crossings are junctions without connecting roads where traffic of two roads crosses but cannot change roads (pedestrians, cyclists, rail). Cross paths (pedestrians/cyclists) let traffic of a lane cross other lanes and continue on a lane of the same or another road. Mid-block pedestrian crossing: virtual junction on the uncut main road with a crossing road and crossPath connecting the two sidewalks. Rail crossing: crossing junction with one roadSection per road and priority for the rail.
guidance: Pedestrian/bike crossing outside a common junction: choose a virtual junction with crossPath (best for linking sidewalks of different roads).
Keep the main road continuous (junction=-1) with its normal lanes (driving, curb, walking).
If there is a refuge island, add a dedicated lane section with a lane of type restricted whose width grows/shrinks (cubic widths) and renumber/link the outer lanes across the sections.
Create the crossing road with its reference line from the middle of one sidewalk walking lane to the middle of the opposite one, with a single walking lane.
Create <junction type="virtual" mainRoad=<main road> sStart sEnd> with sStart/sEnd clearly outside the crossing area.

Add <crossPath crossingRoad=<crossing road> roadAtStart=<road> roadAtEnd=<road>> (same main road at both ends is allowed) with startLaneLink/endLaneLink: s on the start/end road, from = walking lane of that road, to = lane of the crossing road.
Add <priority high=<main road> low=<crossing road>/> (unsignalised crossing priority as modelled in the guideline).
Set junction=<virtual junction id> on the crossing road only.
Rail crossing: use <junction type="crossing">; keep both roads uncut (junction=-1); road lanes driving per direction, rail road one lane of type rail.
Add one <roadSection id roadId sStart sEnd> per road with sStart/sEnd clearly outside the crossing area.
Add <priority high=<rail road> low=<road>/>, then road markings (stop bars, centre lines) and signs (St. Andrew's cross) on the road approaches.

wrong: Cutting the main road into a common junction for a zebra.
Connecting roads at rail crossings (traffic cannot change roads).
sStart/sEnd inside the crossing area.
